Similar to the approach of the divergence smearing correction in 4 . 3 , the detector resolution correction modifies the current two dimensional LMD fit model from equation 28 to
The function Res ( θ rec x , θ rec y , θ MC x , θ MC y ) contains all the information of the detector smearing. Its domain is 4 dimensional and it gives the probability density for reconstructing particles at angles θ rec x θ rec y initially generated at the IP with angles θ MC x θ MC y . Simulations done with PandaRoot can give insight to this resolution function as both the generated and reconstructed angles are available.
There are two possibilities to extract this information from the simulation results and construct a resolution function. The first solution tries to parameterize the resolution as a function of the generated (MC) angles θ MC x θ MC y , by first splitting the simulated resolution information into bins of these angles and then fitting each of these local two dimensional resolution distributions with an appropriate model extracting the resolution parameters. When applying the smearing, the resolution model, here a 2 D normal distribution, is initialized with the correct parameters dependent on the angles θ MC x θ MC y . Unfortunately it turns out that the resolution parameterization is extremely complex, as the resolution is not constant along the generated angles θ MC x θ MC y . Also the resolution at specific θ MC x θ MC y proximities can have additional contributions to the 2 D normal distribution. These complications arise due to an inhomogeneous material budget of the detector and edge effects. The problem of the resolution parameterization can be avoided in the second solution, in which simulation data is used directly by storing the required information within a 4 D histogram. Due to the better compatibility and reliability, the latter solution was chosen. However it imposes other difficulties that are related to statistics and storage. In order to obtain equal statistical uncertainties for the resolution smearing probabilities when increasing the binning or density of these 4 D histograms, the needed amount of data has to be increased with the fourth power. A similar statement holds for the storage of the resolution information, which can quickly exceed several gigabytes. From this point of view the histogram binning constant should be chosen as coarse as possible.
To be able to systematically study this large chain of sophisiticated correction algorithms and allow the flexible extension for further corrections, the need for a framework for the construction of general functions of arbitrary dimensionality and complexity arose. This led to the development of an additional software package, the ModelFramework [ 109 ], which is a dependency of the LuminosityFit software 8 .
8 Both software packages are written purely in C++.

The reason for this is the only partial overlap of the pixels of the front and back sensors, yielding an improved resolution after performing hit merging of the two sides. For lower beam momenta this discrete structure is not visible anymore, as it is smeared by the larger detector resolution from multiple scattering. LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION - THE LUMINOSITY FIT FRAMEWORK
This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. One possibility is to correct the measured data for the effects introduced by the ¯ PANDA spectrometer, which then allows a direct comparison with the pure elastic scattering model. Alternatively, the pure model can be modified to include all of the effects that arise during the measurement, so that is directly comparable with the data. The first option is in practice not feasible as required operations such as deconvolutions, which undo the detector resolution of the data, require very large amounts of data and a constant resolution to work reliably. On these grounds the second option was chosen, allowing for far more flexibility, extraction power and precision. The construction of the fit model with all of the transformations and correction procedures of the elastic scattering cross section is presented in detail in the following. Results on the extracted luminosity precision and studies of systematic uncertainties are presented in the next chapter.
4 . 1 the elastic scattering model
The cross section for elastic ¯ pp scattering was introduced in section 3 . 3 . Apart from the calculable coulomb part of the total elastic cross section, two possible parameterizations for the description of the hadronic part exist. Both parameterizations are implemented in the LuminosityFit software. Despite the fact that the E 760 parameterization is more suitable, because it uses more measurements in the four momentum range of the LMD, the DPM parameterization was chosen for the studies in this thesis (see equation 18 ). The reasoning is that the DPM generator is the only official generator for the ¯ PANDA experiment that includes elastic ¯ pp processes 1 . Moreover the operability of the LuminosityFit software and the validity of its extraction precision and studies on systematic uncertainties are not influenced by the chosen parameterization, as long as the behavior of the true physics cross section is described approximated. To ensure meaningful results of the systematic effects, the parameterization of the event generator and the fit model of the luminosity extraction software are identical.
1 The official version of the DPM generator unfortunately uses 32 bit floating point precision. For the small excerpt of the angular spectrum of the LMD, the numerical precision was not good enough. Therefore a special 64 bit precision version of this generator is used in the simulation studies

LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION RESULTS AND SYSTEMATIC STUDIES
This chapter presents the performance and accuracy of the LuminosityFit framework including systematic studies of the influence of the accelerator and target beam parameterization on the accuracy. At first the runtime settings of the luminosity fit are given followed by results of the luminosity determination for the ideal scenario. In this scenario merely the parameterizations of the accelerator beam momentum and IP distributions are idealistic, which use delta functions δ 3 ( ⃗ p lab ) with ⃗ p lab = ( 0 , 0 , p lab ) and δ 3 ( ⃗ IP ) with ⃗ IP = ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) . The parameters for realistic distributions are the shift and width of the IP distribution and the tilt and divergence of the accelerator beam. They are studied systematically, with both expected parameter values as well as an extreme case. Those values are taken from section 2 . 2 . 1 , in which these parameters are discussed and summarized.
Because the detector resolutions (figure 32 ) and elastic scattering cross sections (figure 25 ) between the lab momenta of 4 . 06 GeV and 15 GeV/c are similar, most of the following studies were only performed for the two extreme values for the antiproton beam momentum of 1 . 5 GeV/c and 15 GeV/c . However results of several realistic scenarios with non-trivial accelerator and target beam parameters as well as different beam momenta are shown afterwards.
All data shown in this chapter has been simulated with the PandaRoot framework with only pure elastic ¯ pp scattering events and no background from inelastic channels. All relevant background sources are discussed at the end of this chapter.
5 . 1 ideal case fit results
Before any fit results are shown, some general information on the determination procedure has to be provided. The fits are performed with the LuminosityFit software using an extended binned log-likelihood estimator. With the typical data sample size of 10 6 events and a 2 D histogram binning of roughly 300 in each dimension a binned estimator is favored.
It was discovered that fits with a chi-square estimator give a systematic error on the luminosity in the order of 0 . 1 %. The reason for this is the assumption of a normal distributed bin content, which is not well enough satisfied for the used sample sizes and poisson statistics is preferable [ 110 ]. This systematic error mainly effects the normalization constant, but for the luminosity determination this is precisely the crucial parameter. A complete description of the likelihood estimator is given in section A. 1 .
When using a binned estimator it is important to compare the bin content with the integral of the model within the bin boundaries. This is in general a quite computation expensive calculation, especially if the model changes with the fit parameters. In the limit of fine binnings the function can be regarded as constant within the boundaries of a single bin and a single function evaluation normalized to the area of bin provides an accurate value for the integral. The two dimensional integrals for the luminosity fit are calculated by evaluating the model on a 3 × 3 grid within each bin, giving the necessary precision without large speed penalties. These integrals are cached and the luminosity fit model is now discretized according to the histogram of the data.

The Luminosity Fit Framework
65
Designed with a strict Object-Oriented architecture, the framework prioritizes modularity and flexibility. It decouples the physics implementation from the numerical optimization engine and the data storage backend. This separation of concerns allows for the seamless interchange of interaction models (e.g., different cross section parametrizations) or minimization algorithms without modifying the core analysis logic.
Architectural Design
The framework is structured around a central orchestration layer, utilizing the Facade Design Pattern to manage the interaction between four abstract components:
Data Representation Layer: Experimental data and Monte Carlo simulations after the full track reconstruction procedure in Section 3.4 are encapsulated into a unified histogram interface. This abstraction layer handles the binning of the angular phase space in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 , defined as 𝜃 𝑥 ≈ 𝑝 𝑥 /𝑝 𝑧 and 𝜃 𝑦 ≈ 𝑝 𝑦 /𝑝 𝑧 for small angles) and provides coherent access to bin contents and statistical errors. By isolating the analysis from the underlying file format (e.g., ROOT Trees), the fit performance is optimized for high-statistics datasets.
Abstract Model Interface: The physics of the scattering process is defined through a generalized model interface. Concrete implementations (e.g., the DPM) provide the probability density functions (PDF). Crucially, this layer is responsible for the 'Forward-Folding' process: it accounts for the detector acceptance, which incorporates the beam shift effects, and convolves the theoretical cross section (as shown in Figure 3.4) with the detector resolution and beam smearing effects during the fit.
Estimator Strategy: The quantification of the agreement between the model and the data is handled by an interchangeable estimator component. While standard 𝜒 2 metrics are available for diagnostics, the primary analysis utilizes a Binned Log-Likelihood estimator. This approach is statistically required to correctly treat low-statistics bins in the high-| 𝑡 | tail of the distribution.
Minimization Backend: The numerical optimization of the likelihood function is delegated to an external engine wrapper. This design allows the framework to utilize robust third-party libraries (such as Minuit2 ) to find the global minimum in the multi-dimensional parameter space efficiently.

Here, 𝜖 𝑖 represents the geometrical acceptance map, 𝐵 𝑖 is the background term, and 𝑅 is the resolution function. The symbol ⊗ denotes the numerical convolution of the theoretical cross section with the detector resolution. By modeling these effects explicitly, the software ensures that the extracted parameters are free from detector-induced biases.
IP Alignment and Coordinate Transformation
A critical pre-processing step implemented in the framework is the alignment of the coordinate system. The standard laboratory frame assumes the interaction point is at (0 , 0 , 0). However, real beam operations imply a transverse offset ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ).
The framework utilizes the full 3D tracking information available after the backpropagation step to determine this offset geometrically. For each back-propagated track, the Point of Closest Approach (POCA) relative to the nominal coordinate origin (0 , 0 , 0) (or given point ( 𝑥 𝑖 , 𝑦 𝑖 , 0) taken from other detectors) is calculated. This results in a distribution of interaction vertices in the transverse plane. The arithmetic mean of these POCA coordinates is identified as the measurement of the mean interaction point ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0). Before the luminosity fit, a global coordinate transformation is applied to all track data:
This virtually shifts the detector system such that the interaction point coincides with the origin, restoring the azimuthal symmetry required for the 2D luminosity fit model.
Detector Response Modeling
The raw angular distribution measured by the LMD differs from the theoretical cross-section due to two distinct instrumental effects: the limited geometrical acceptance and the finite angular resolution. In the LuminosityFit framework, these effects are decoupled and treated sequentially using a forward-folding approach.
The Acceptance 𝜖 represents the probability that an elastic scattering event is successfully detected and reconstructed. Due to the planar geometry of the HV-MAPS, the acceptance structures (such as sensor edges, overlaps, and module gaps) are most naturally described in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ).
The acceptance map 𝜖 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) is generated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations. A sample of 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 single track events is generated utilizing a Box Generator and processed through the full Geant4 detector simulation and tracking chain to obtain the number of reconstructed tracks ( 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐 ) independence on the coordinates

4 . 5 detector resolution smearing
Finally the imprecision of the measured track parameters by the LMD, more specifically the angles θ x θ y , has to be taken into account. This finite resolution for the angles arises mainly from two factors. The reconstructed track hits vary from the true values because of the intrinsic sensor resolution and the multiple scattering in the modules and the transition cone. The latter is dominant at low beam energies. Figure 31 shows the two dimensional angular resolution distributions for the two extreme momenta of the ¯ PANDA experiment. It can be seen that the resolution distributions can be rotated and skewed, because of the solenoid and dipole magnetic fields. By fitting the resolution distributions of various beam momenta with a 2 D multivariate gaussian model, the parameters of the resolution as a function of the momentum in the laboratory frame can be extracted and are depicted in figure 32 . Clearly the dominance of multiple scattering towards lower energies is visualized by the increase of the width of the resolution distributions, which are an effect of the reduced track 'stiffness' for lower momentum antiprotons.

Condition-Specific MC Production: The determined IP parameters (mean offset and beam width from HESR) serve as input for a dedicated Monte Carlo simulation. These simulations with single track events generate the Acceptance Map 𝜖 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) and determine the Resolution Function 𝑅 𝑑𝑒𝑡 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ). This step is crucial: by customizing the MC samples to the observed beam parameters, the geometrical acceptance corrections implicitly include the effects of the beam offset and width.

Fit Model Construction: Simultaneously, the theoretical differential crosssection 𝑑𝜎 𝑑 Ω is calculated using the DPM model for the relevant beam momentum. The fit model is constructed by convolving the theory with the resolution and multiplying by the acceptance. Figure 3.12 (right) shows the final 2D DPM model.

Neglecting this tilt induces a spurious 𝜑 -dependence in the data. The measured polar angle 𝜃 𝑙𝑎𝑏 would be systematically shifted depending on 𝜑 , distorting the 𝑡 -distribution and ruining the fit quality. The LuminosityFit framework treats the Beam Tilt as a coordinate transformation. The reconstructed momentum vectors of all tracks are rotated from the 'Laboratory Frame' into the 'Beam Reference Frame' using a rotation matrix 𝑅 ( 𝑡 𝑥 , 𝑡 𝑦 ), effectively aligning the effective beam axis with the 𝑧 -axis for the analysis, which define the variables 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 :
Beam Divergence
In contrast to the coherent tilt, the Beam Divergence represents the intrinsic statistical spread of the particle directions within the beam bunch. It follows a Gaussian distribution with width 𝜎 𝑑𝑖𝑣 . Since the initial direction of a specific antiproton is unknown, this effect cannot be corrected event-by-event. Instead, it acts as an irreducible angular smearing.
In the luminosity fit model, the beam divergence is treated by convolution. It adds in quadrature to the detector's intrinsic resolution 𝑅 𝑑𝑒𝑡 . The total effective resolution kernel 𝑅 𝑒𝑓𝑓 is given by:

3.6 Effects of Beam Properties
In the ideal mathematical description of elastic scattering, the interaction occurs at a singular point (0 , 0 , 0) and the antiproton beam vector is perfectly aligned with the 𝑧 -axis. However, the realistic PANDA beam conditions at the HESR introduce geometric and kinematic deviations. To achieve the target precision for the luminosity determination, these effects must be rigorously modeled to avoid systematic biases. They can be categorized into deterministic mean shifts, shift and tilt as illustrated in Figure 3.10, and stochastic broadening (Divergence). The IP Offset , shown in green, shifts the primary vertex position away from the nominal detector center, thereby breaking the azimuthal symmetry of the tracks. Furthermore, the Beam Tilt , shown in blue, causes a systematic angular deviation that strongly depends on the azimuthal angle 𝜑 .
IP Offset and Distribution
The interaction zone is defined by the spatial overlap of the antiproton beam and the target stream. This creates a distributed source rather than a point source. The framework treats the mean position (Offset) and the profile width of this distribution differently based on the detector's sensitivity. A transverse displacement ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ) of the beam breaks the azimuthal symmetry of the detector acceptance. To determine this offset precisely, the Back-Propagation procedure is exploited as described in Section 3.4. After extrapolating the reconstructed tracks through the magnetic field back to the target region, the geometrical origin of each track is determined by calculating its Point of Closest Approach (POCA) to the nominal coordinate origin (0 , 0 , 0). The spatial distribution of these POCA points reflects the beam spot profile smeared by the resolution from reconstruction precision. Nevertheless, the Mean of this distribution provides the mean interaction vertex ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0) with high precision ( 𝒪 (10 𝜇 m)). This measured position is then used to define the 'Beam Reference Frame'. All reconstructed quantities are calculated relative to this physically determined center, effectively removing the systematic bias induced by the beam offset.

For the LMD analysis, the Cellular Automaton algorithm is the preferred choice [92]. The implementation used in this work creates track candidates requiring hits in at least 3 out of 4 stations to ensure high efficiency while suppressing ghost tracks.
Track Fitting with GenFit
Once track candidates are found, their kinematic parameters must be estimated. The reconstruction utilizes the GenFit toolkit [130], which supports multiple fitting algorithms, most notably the General Broken Lines (GBL) [131, 132] fit and the Kalman Filter [133, 134].
General Broken Lines (GBL) The GBL algorithm constructs a trajectory from a sequence of thin scatterers. It is particularly powerful for detector alignment as it provides explicit access to the residuals of all measurements simultaneously.
Kalman Filter The Kalman filter is a recursive estimator that updates the track state vector ⃗ 𝑞 = ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧, 𝑝 𝑥 , 𝑝 𝑦 , 𝑝 𝑧 ) at each measurement plane. It is the preferred algorithm for track reconstruction due to its superior handling of complex material effects. Specifically, it incorporates deterministic energy dissipation governed by the Bethe-Bloch formula when particles traverse the detector sensors and support structures. Furthermore, the filter elegantly accounts for Multiple Coulomb Scattering (MCS) by treating it as stochastic process noise. This approach appropriately inflates the track's covariance matrix, accurately reflecting the accumulated spatial uncertainties induced by the detector's material budget.
For the determination of the luminosity, the Kalman Filter is selected as the primary fitting algorithm. This ensures that the final error estimates at the first detector layer are statistically rigorous, which is a prerequisite for the accurate back-propagation to the interaction point.
Back-Propagation to the Interaction Point
For luminosity determination, the physics observable is the scattering angle 𝜃 at the Interaction Point ( 𝑧 = 0), not at the detector ( 𝑧 ≈ 11 m). Between the IP and the LMD, the antiprotons traverse the stray field of the solenoid and the strong dipole magnet field, which deflects trajectories horizontally. To recover the true scattering angle, the fitted tracks must be propagated backwards using the GEANE track propagator [135, 136]. This step involves a subtle but critical assumption regarding the particle momentum.

The function Res ( θ rec x , θ rec y , θ MC x , θ MC y ) contains all the information of the detector smearing. Its domain is 4 dimensional and it gives the probability density for reconstructing particles at angles θ rec x θ rec y initially generated at the IP with angles θ MC x θ MC y . Simulations done with PandaRoot can give insight to this resolution function as both the generated and reconstructed angles are available.
There are two possibilities to extract this information from the simulation results and construct a resolution function. The first solution tries to parameterize the resolution as a function of the generated (MC) angles θ MC x θ MC y , by first splitting the simulated resolution information into bins of these angles and then fitting each of these local two dimensional resolution distributions with an appropriate model extracting the resolution parameters. When applying the smearing, the resolution model, here a 2 D normal distribution, is initialized with the correct parameters dependent on the angles θ MC x θ MC y . Unfortunately it turns out that the resolution parameterization is extremely complex, as the resolution is not constant along the generated angles θ MC x θ MC y . Also the resolution at specific θ MC x θ MC y proximities can have additional contributions to the 2 D normal distribution. These complications arise due to an inhomogeneous material budget of the detector and edge effects. The problem of the resolution parameterization can be avoided in the second solution, in which simulation data is used directly by storing the required information within a 4 D histogram. Due to the better compatibility and reliability, the latter solution was chosen. However it imposes other difficulties that are related to statistics and storage. In order to obtain equal statistical uncertainties for the resolution smearing probabilities when increasing the binning or density of these 4 D histograms, the needed amount of data has to be increased with the fourth power. A similar statement holds for the storage of the resolution information, which can quickly exceed several gigabytes. From this point of view the histogram binning constant should be chosen as coarse as possible.
To be able to systematically study this large chain of sophisiticated correction algorithms and allow the flexible extension for further corrections, the need for a framework for the construction of general functions of arbitrary dimensionality and complexity arose. This led to the development of an additional software package, the ModelFramework [ 109 ], which is a dependency of the LuminosityFit software 8 .

The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. The superior vertexing resolution and reduced material budget of the sensors are critical factors that enable the effective determination of the Restgas distribution even for interactions significantly displaced from the nominal IP.
Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the systematic distortions caused by resolution smearing and initial model inaccuracies are rigorously suppressed. This method acts as a contracting map, converging to the true physical distribution and ensuring that the final result is independent of the initial simulation input provided by the Target Group. To quantify the stability of this approach, an iterative procedure was initialized with an extreme starting condition: a 40% overestimation of the Restgas distribution. As summarized in Table 9.1, the iterative procedure converges rapidly. Within merely three steps, the global deviation drops from 12 . 27% to 1 . 30%, and the deviation in the central region vanishes to -0 . 22%. Consequently, the precise density profile can be derived directly from the experimental data across the entire relevant domain, providing the reliable input essential for the absolute luminosity determination.
Finally, the determined Restgas profile was integrated back into the LuminosityFit framework to validate the complete analysis chain. The luminosity determination was performed at a beam momentum of 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , applying a cut within the analysis window ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 1 cm and | 𝑧 | < 5 cm). The relative deviation of the determined luminosity (Δ ℒ / ℒ ) is (0 . 05 ± 0 . 07)% with the reconstructed target profile with Restgas background. As presented in Table 9.2, this result is consistent with the ideal case where the target is treated as point-like and the efficiency correction is based on a point-like model, which yields a deviation of -0 . 036 ± 0 . 07% and also with the case where the target profile with Restgas background is well-known and totally the same as real data, which yields a deviation of 0 . 02 ± 0 . 08%. This results demonstrate that the synergy of high-precision tracking and advanced fitting algorithms transforms the Restgas background from a limiting systematic background into a precisely monitored observable, enabling a robust and accurate luminosity determination for the PANDA experiment.

Summary and Outlook
The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) represents the future precision frontier of hadron physics, addressing fundamental questions regarding the strong interaction, including the search for gluonic excitations, the spectroscopy of charmonium states, and the investigation of nucleon structure. A prerequisite for fully exploiting this discovery potential-particularly for the measurement of absolute cross-sections and the scanning of narrow resonance lineshapes-is the precise determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While the primary luminosity measurement relies on the detection of antiproton-proton elastic scattering in the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference region, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixed-target setup introduce significant challenges that render conventional point-source approximations insufficient. Specifically, the interaction of the antiproton beam with the Restgas background distributed along the beam pipe creates a non-localized background source which, if not correctly modeled, fundamentally limits the attainable experimental precision.
To overcome these limitations, this thesis established a comprehensive methodology that transforms the handling of the extended interaction region from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. Central to this approach was the refinement of the object-oriented software framework LuminosityFit , which implements a rigorous convolution model combining the theoretical differential cross-section with the detector's resolution and geometric acceptance. By incorporating a Dual Parton Model (DPM) to accurately describe the hadronic amplitude and introducing the concept of an 'Effective Acceptance Map', the framework successfully integrates the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap into the fitting procedure. Extensive validation studies demonstrated that this algorithmic approach robustly decouples the luminosity signal from background contributions induced by beam systematics, effectively correcting for beam tilts, transverse offsets, and statistical divergence to recover the input luminosity with a relative statistical precision of better than 0.5%. However, sensitivity analysis revealed a critical dependency: the accuracy of the extraction is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. A deviation of 10% in the assumed Restgas model was shown to induce a systematic luminosity bias of approximately 3.4%, a magnitude that exceeds the stringent precision requirements necessary for the PANDA physics program.
To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION - THE LUMINOSITY FIT FRAMEWORK
This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. One possibility is to correct the measured data for the effects introduced by the ¯ PANDA spectrometer, which then allows a direct comparison with the pure elastic scattering model. Alternatively, the pure model can be modified to include all of the effects that arise during the measurement, so that is directly comparable with the data. The first option is in practice not feasible as required operations such as deconvolutions, which undo the detector resolution of the data, require very large amounts of data and a constant resolution to work reliably. On these grounds the second option was chosen, allowing for far more flexibility, extraction power and precision. The construction of the fit model with all of the transformations and correction procedures of the elastic scattering cross section is presented in detail in the following. Results on the extracted luminosity precision and studies of systematic uncertainties are presented in the next chapter.
4 . 1 the elastic scattering model
The cross section for elastic ¯ pp scattering was introduced in section 3 . 3 . Apart from the calculable coulomb part of the total elastic cross section, two possible parameterizations for the description of the hadronic part exist. Both parameterizations are implemented in the LuminosityFit software. Despite the fact that the E 760 parameterization is more suitable, because it uses more measurements in the four momentum range of the LMD, the DPM parameterization was chosen for the studies in this thesis (see equation 18 ). The reasoning is that the DPM generator is the only official generator for the ¯ PANDA experiment that includes elastic ¯ pp processes 1 . Moreover the operability of the LuminosityFit software and the validity of its extraction precision and studies on systematic uncertainties are not influenced by the chosen parameterization, as long as the behavior of the true physics cross section is described approximated. To ensure meaningful results of the systematic effects, the parameterization of the event generator and the fit model of the luminosity extraction software are identical.

8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

A collection of (mostly) Python3 scripts to facilitate the use of the LuminosityFit software.

Note that the whole workflow is far from trivial, and there are many details that are not mentioned in this Readme.

The LuminosityFit software requires a reconstructed elastic scattering events from the Panda Luminosity Detector (LMD).

As long as the [PANDA experiment](https://panda.gsi.de/) is not running these events have to be simulated using the PandaRoot framework.

Simulations and reconstruction can be easily performed using the python scripts `doSimulationReconstruction.py` or `doReconstruction.py`. Use the `--help` flag to get more detailed information on how to use these scripts. These scripts create so call configuration files `sim_params.config` and `reco_params.config`, that contain all of the information to perform a simulation or reconstruction (as you specified them).

The are useful for bookkeeping and can also be used to redo the simulation or reconstruction using the scripts `runSimulationReconstruction.py` and `runReconstruction.py`.

Note that the simulation step also can create an `elastic_cross_section.txt` file when the dpm mode is selected. It contains the cross section of the elastic scattering process, corresponding to the generated events. From this the reference luminosity can be calculated, which is useful for calculating the accuracy of the luminosity determination procedure.

Once you have an unfiltered (do **NOT** use any cut flags in the reconstruction, such as `--use_xy_cut` or `--use_m_cut`) dataset of reconstructed elastic scattering events, the luminosity determination can be started.

Use `determineLuminosity.py`, which is quite complicated and *fragile*, and only runs on the Himster2 cluster in Mainz. The reason for this is that the whole luminosity determination process is very difficult. The excellent accuracy in the below percent level can only be reached with big efforts. Currently the efficiency and resolution corrections are performed via additional simulations and reconstruction.

The overall steps in the luminosity determination process are:

1. create interaction point (IP) distribution from the unfiltered reconstructed elastic scattering tracks
2. determine the means (X,Y,Z) of the IP distribution
3. filter the elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently do a simulation and reconstruction using the determined IP info and a box generator
4. create a 2D angular track distribution of the filtered elastic scattering dataset 
   **AND** independently create an efficiency and a resolution object from the box generated dataset
5. perform the actual luminosity fit using the 2D angular track distribution and the efficiency and resolution objects

These step exclude a possible alignment process which should run before all of this.

SUMMARY
Several aspects of the strong interaction still remain nebulous, despite large efforts over decades. In the low energy regime, the classification of the bound states and deciphering their structure prove to be difficult in certain areas of the hadron spectrum. Due to the unique properties of the strong interaction, the meson spectrum cannot be calculated analytically and effective models are used. Precise measurements of these bound states and their properties are important, in order to test the validity of the theoretical models. The mass and width of the 0 ++ isoscalars are difficult to extract experimentally, because multiple wide and overlapping states are present. This region is particularly interesting, since there are more states than expected by the constituent quark model and a light glueball state is predicted here by lattice-QCD calculations. Also the unexpected X, Y, Z states in the charmonium sector are compelling, as they are candidates with exotic content with respect to the regular meson quark-antiquark contribution.
One highly accurate method to determine the line shape, i. e. the mass and width, of states is the energy scan. The knowledge of the luminosity is essential to normalize the measured line shape. The energy scans will be performed by the future precision experiment ¯ PANDA, for which the luminosity detector (LMD) measures the luminosity. When determining the properties of a broader spectrum of states, the partial wave analysis (PWA) is of great importance. This method allows for the extraction of additional quantum numbers such as the spin and parity. In the 0 ++ isoscalar sector the precise extraction of state masses and widths is hindered by complicated structure of the dynamics. The usual Breit-Wigner parameterization reaches its limits here. To obtain a measure on the ability of a theoretical model to describe the measured data, a comparison of the results with other models is important. This is one of the goals of the ComPWA project, which intends to provide various formalisms and models.
The first part of the thesis was the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible accuracy and precision for the ¯ PANDA experiment from the track information of the LMD. For this the versatile LuminosityFit software was developed, providing reliable and accurate luminosity information. Numerous effects influence the stability and accuracy of the luminosity extraction procedure, for which extensive studies were performed. These are the track reconstruction efficiency, the detector resolution, and all effects arising from the distribution and displacement of the IP, as well as the tilt and divergence of the accelerator beam. Furthermore the implementation and performance of the accordant correction algorithms are presented. They enable the high accuracy of the luminosity that is extracted with the fit software. Altogether the luminosity is determined with an accuracy of about 0 . 5 %for beam momenta up to 5 GeV/c and 0 . 1 %for the above higher momentum regime.

Designed with a strict Object-Oriented architecture, the framework prioritizes modularity and flexibility. It decouples the physics implementation from the numerical optimization engine and the data storage backend. This separation of concerns allows for the seamless interchange of interaction models (e.g., different cross section parametrizations) or minimization algorithms without modifying the core analysis logic.
Architectural Design
The framework is structured around a central orchestration layer, utilizing the Facade Design Pattern to manage the interaction between four abstract components:
Data Representation Layer: Experimental data and Monte Carlo simulations after the full track reconstruction procedure in Section 3.4 are encapsulated into a unified histogram interface. This abstraction layer handles the binning of the angular phase space in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 , defined as 𝜃 𝑥 ≈ 𝑝 𝑥 /𝑝 𝑧 and 𝜃 𝑦 ≈ 𝑝 𝑦 /𝑝 𝑧 for small angles) and provides coherent access to bin contents and statistical errors. By isolating the analysis from the underlying file format (e.g., ROOT Trees), the fit performance is optimized for high-statistics datasets.
Abstract Model Interface: The physics of the scattering process is defined through a generalized model interface. Concrete implementations (e.g., the DPM) provide the probability density functions (PDF). Crucially, this layer is responsible for the 'Forward-Folding' process: it accounts for the detector acceptance, which incorporates the beam shift effects, and convolves the theoretical cross section (as shown in Figure 3.4) with the detector resolution and beam smearing effects during the fit.
Estimator Strategy: The quantification of the agreement between the model and the data is handled by an interchangeable estimator component. While standard 𝜒 2 metrics are available for diagnostics, the primary analysis utilizes a Binned Log-Likelihood estimator. This approach is statistically required to correctly treat low-statistics bins in the high-| 𝑡 | tail of the distribution.
Minimization Backend: The numerical optimization of the likelihood function is delegated to an external engine wrapper. This design allows the framework to utilize robust third-party libraries (such as Minuit2 ) to find the global minimum in the multi-dimensional parameter space efficiently.

Obviously for position changes of the IP the angular distribution of the scattering process is not effected. However even though the scattering angles of the outgoing antiprotons are identical, the paths of the individual particles through the experimental setup are now different. As a consequence, the detector efficiency changes since previously reconstructed particles on the edge of the detector may now miss the sensor planes and vice versa. It is crucial that the magnetic field maps of the PandaRoot software represent the magnetic fields of the experiment, otherwise systematic errors in the luminosity determination can occur. The ¯ PANDA experiment will perform a high precision scan measurement of the magnetic fields [ 111 ]. Hence this influence is classified as uncritical.
For an incoming particle with an inclination to the z -axis, its scattering angle in the laboratory system θ ′ now differs from the one of the physics process θ . The physics and laboratory coordinate systems are no longer aligned, hence the angular distribution of a scattering process is directly effected. However only the amount of particles scattered into the angular elements change and the individual particle paths remain the same. Therefore the detector acceptance remains unchanged. Strictly speaking the antiproton paths originating from the same angular scattering region before and after a tilt may vary, since they have different momenta due to the different momentum transfer to the proton.
In general this shift and tilt is different for each event and will follow distributions described by the IP distribution and accelerator beam divergence.
5 . 2 . 1 IP Distribution
The IP distribution is the overlap of the accelerator beam distribution and the target beam distribution, while mean displacements of the IP distribution are neglegted in this section. For a correct description one relies on the information of these two distributions, either from simulations or measurements. For the accelerator beam position a normal distribution in the xy plane is used. Estimations on the accelerator beam parameters are summarized in tables 2 and 3 . For the target beams there are two possible systems, the cluster jet target and pellet target. As the former will be used in the beginning of the ¯ PANDA runtime and measurements for the target beam distribution exist, this system was chosen in this study. The target hydrogen clusters follow the distribution given in equation 6 , with a slightly elongated shape in the z direction, while newest measurements even suggest a wider gaussian distribution[ 112 ]. Because the antiproton beam is costly to create and high reaction rates are desired, the target beam is usually broadened in the xy plane to have a good overlap with the antiproton beam. Therefore the dimensions of the IP distribution in the x and y direction are dictated by the size of the more narrow accelerator beam when performing the overlap. Hence a normal distribution for x and y with widths of σ x = σ y = 0 . 8 mm is used. Along the beam direction the distribution is dominated by the target beam profile and would be described best by equation 6 . However for reasons of simplicity a gaussian distribution with a similar width was used instead. The 2σ interval of the normal distribution should roughly equal the 13 . 1 mm size in z direction, therefore 4σ z ≈ 13 . 1 mm → σ z = 3 . 5 mm . The distribution of the pellet target beam is similar in xy , and therefore also the IP distribution parameterization.

Similar to the approach of the divergence smearing correction in 4 . 3 , the detector resolution correction modifies the current two dimensional LMD fit model from equation 28 to
The function Res ( θ rec x , θ rec y , θ MC x , θ MC y ) contains all the information of the detector smearing. Its domain is 4 dimensional and it gives the probability density for reconstructing particles at angles θ rec x θ rec y initially generated at the IP with angles θ MC x θ MC y . Simulations done with PandaRoot can give insight to this resolution function as both the generated and reconstructed angles are available.
There are two possibilities to extract this information from the simulation results and construct a resolution function. The first solution tries to parameterize the resolution as a function of the generated (MC) angles θ MC x θ MC y , by first splitting the simulated resolution information into bins of these angles and then fitting each of these local two dimensional resolution distributions with an appropriate model extracting the resolution parameters. When applying the smearing, the resolution model, here a 2 D normal distribution, is initialized with the correct parameters dependent on the angles θ MC x θ MC y . Unfortunately it turns out that the resolution parameterization is extremely complex, as the resolution is not constant along the generated angles θ MC x θ MC y . Also the resolution at specific θ MC x θ MC y proximities can have additional contributions to the 2 D normal distribution. These complications arise due to an inhomogeneous material budget of the detector and edge effects. The problem of the resolution parameterization can be avoided in the second solution, in which simulation data is used directly by storing the required information within a 4 D histogram. Due to the better compatibility and reliability, the latter solution was chosen. However it imposes other difficulties that are related to statistics and storage. In order to obtain equal statistical uncertainties for the resolution smearing probabilities when increasing the binning or density of these 4 D histograms, the needed amount of data has to be increased with the fourth power. A similar statement holds for the storage of the resolution information, which can quickly exceed several gigabytes. From this point of view the histogram binning constant should be chosen as coarse as possible.
To be able to systematically study this large chain of sophisiticated correction algorithms and allow the flexible extension for further corrections, the need for a framework for the construction of general functions of arbitrary dimensionality and complexity arose. This led to the development of an additional software package, the ModelFramework [ 109 ], which is a dependency of the LuminosityFit software 8 .

In reality the number of scattered anti-protons inside an angular element ∆θ at an angle θ rec is measured. This is described by equation 103 .
Here dσ ( θmc ) dθmc is the probability that the antiproton was scattered into a infinitesimal θ ring element ∆θ mc at a certain θ mc value. Propagating this particle through the magnetic fields and/or material, eventually the particle may leave behind signals in the detectors. ϵ ( θ mc ) describes the probability, that the particle within the angular element ∆θ mc at a specific value of θ mc is actually reconstructed. Finally due to the detector resolution and scattering effects in material, the reconstructed angle θ rec deviates from the true angle θ mc . The probability for a particle within the angular element ∆θ mc at θ mc to be reconstructed at an angle θ rec within ∆θ rec is given by dRes ( θrec -θmc , θmc ) dθrec . To obtain the probability of measuring scattered antiprotons inside an angular element ∆θ at an angle θ rec , an integral over all initial scattering angles has to be performed. To obtain the number of particles scattered into this angular element within a unit of time, the overall probability has to be scaled with the time-integrated luminosity. Putting everything together one ends up with equation 103 .
For the special case that dRes ( θrec -θmc , θmc ) dθrec only depends on the difference θ rec -θ mc , equation 103 can be simplified to 104 .
In this case the integral over θ mc turned into the convolution expressed by the operator ∗ . Figure 86 visualizes the equality in this special case. Here the red curve is the probability density function dσ ( θmc ) dθmc · ϵ ( θ mc ) of particles scattered at an angles θ mc and leave behind information to be reconstructed by the detector. The black and black dashed curves are normal distributions with equal widths, which resemble the resolution of the detector dRes ( θrec -θmc ) dθrec . Note that the width of the normal distributions was set to this arbitrary large value to clarify the mathematical concept. The overall probability of measuring a particle in the neighborhood of θ rec = 2 . 5mrad , that originated from the vicinity of θ mc = 4 . 0mrad , is calculated by the product of the values of the red and black-dashed functions at these positions. On the other hand the solid black curve shows the same normal function shifted to the position of 2 . 5mrad . Evaluating this function at 4 . 0mrad , one can see that the probability is equal to the dashed black curve at 2 . 5mrad . Integrating over all possible θ mc , the overall probability is obtained. The integral of the product of the solid black and red curve is the convolution of these functions evaluated at the position 2 . 5mrad .

Finally the imprecision of the measured track parameters by the LMD, more specifically the angles θ x θ y , has to be taken into account. This finite resolution for the angles arises mainly from two factors. The reconstructed track hits vary from the true values because of the intrinsic sensor resolution and the multiple scattering in the modules and the transition cone. The latter is dominant at low beam energies. Figure 31 shows the two dimensional angular resolution distributions for the two extreme momenta of the ¯ PANDA experiment. It can be seen that the resolution distributions can be rotated and skewed, because of the solenoid and dipole magnetic fields. By fitting the resolution distributions of various beam momenta with a 2 D multivariate gaussian model, the parameters of the resolution as a function of the momentum in the laboratory frame can be extracted and are depicted in figure 32 . Clearly the dominance of multiple scattering towards lower energies is visualized by the increase of the width of the resolution distributions, which are an effect of the reduced track 'stiffness' for lower momentum antiprotons.

From the spacing between the detector planes, which is either 20 cm or 10 cm , the angular resolution of the detector is limited to 80 µ m/20cm = 0 . 4 mrad . The Luminosity Fit Framework
65
Designed with a strict Object-Oriented architecture, the framework prioritizes modularity and flexibility. It decouples the physics implementation from the numerical optimization engine and the data storage backend. This separation of concerns allows for the seamless interchange of interaction models (e.g., different cross section parametrizations) or minimization algorithms without modifying the core analysis logic.
Architectural Design
The framework is structured around a central orchestration layer, utilizing the Facade Design Pattern to manage the interaction between four abstract components:
Data Representation Layer: Experimental data and Monte Carlo simulations after the full track reconstruction procedure in Section 3.4 are encapsulated into a unified histogram interface. This abstraction layer handles the binning of the angular phase space in the projected angular coordinates ( 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 , defined as 𝜃 𝑥 ≈ 𝑝 𝑥 /𝑝 𝑧 and 𝜃 𝑦 ≈ 𝑝 𝑦 /𝑝 𝑧 for small angles) and provides coherent access to bin contents and statistical errors. By isolating the analysis from the underlying file format (e.g., ROOT Trees), the fit performance is optimized for high-statistics datasets.
Abstract Model Interface: The physics of the scattering process is defined through a generalized model interface. Concrete implementations (e.g., the DPM) provide the probability density functions (PDF). Crucially, this layer is responsible for the 'Forward-Folding' process: it accounts for the detector acceptance, which incorporates the beam shift effects, and convolves the theoretical cross section (as shown in Figure 3.4) with the detector resolution and beam smearing effects during the fit.
Estimator Strategy: The quantification of the agreement between the model and the data is handled by an interchangeable estimator component. While standard 𝜒 2 metrics are available for diagnostics, the primary analysis utilizes a Binned Log-Likelihood estimator. This approach is statistically required to correctly treat low-statistics bins in the high-| 𝑡 | tail of the distribution.
Minimization Backend: The numerical optimization of the likelihood function is delegated to an external engine wrapper. This design allows the framework to utilize robust third-party libraries (such as Minuit2 ) to find the global minimum in the multi-dimensional parameter space efficiently.

4
LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION - THE LUMINOSITY FIT FRAMEWORK
This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. One possibility is to correct the measured data for the effects introduced by the ¯ PANDA spectrometer, which then allows a direct comparison with the pure elastic scattering model. Alternatively, the pure model can be modified to include all of the effects that arise during the measurement, so that is directly comparable with the data. The first option is in practice not feasible as required operations such as deconvolutions, which undo the detector resolution of the data, require very large amounts of data and a constant resolution to work reliably. On these grounds the second option was chosen, allowing for far more flexibility, extraction power and precision. The construction of the fit model with all of the transformations and correction procedures of the elastic scattering cross section is presented in detail in the following. Results on the extracted luminosity precision and studies of systematic uncertainties are presented in the next chapter.
4 . 1 the elastic scattering model
The cross section for elastic ¯ pp scattering was introduced in section 3 . 3 . Apart from the calculable coulomb part of the total elastic cross section, two possible parameterizations for the description of the hadronic part exist. Both parameterizations are implemented in the LuminosityFit software. LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION RESULTS AND SYSTEMATIC STUDIES
This chapter presents the performance and accuracy of the LuminosityFit framework including systematic studies of the influence of the accelerator and target beam parameterization on the accuracy. At first the runtime settings of the luminosity fit are given followed by results of the luminosity determination for the ideal scenario. In this scenario merely the parameterizations of the accelerator beam momentum and IP distributions are idealistic, which use delta functions δ 3 ( ⃗ p lab ) with ⃗ p lab = ( 0 , 0 , p lab ) and δ 3 ( ⃗ IP ) with ⃗ IP = ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) . The parameters for realistic distributions are the shift and width of the IP distribution and the tilt and divergence of the accelerator beam. They are studied systematically, with both expected parameter values as well as an extreme case. Those values are taken from section 2 . 2 . 1 , in which these parameters are discussed and summarized.
Because the detector resolutions (figure 32 ) and elastic scattering cross sections (figure 25 ) between the lab momenta of 4 . 06 GeV and 15 GeV/c are similar, most of the following studies were only performed for the two extreme values for the antiproton beam momentum of 1 . 5 GeV/c and 15 GeV/c . However results of several realistic scenarios with non-trivial accelerator and target beam parameters as well as different beam momenta are shown afterwards.
All data shown in this chapter has been simulated with the PandaRoot framework with only pure elastic ¯ pp scattering events and no background from inelastic channels. All relevant background sources are discussed at the end of this chapter.
5 . 1 ideal case fit results
Before any fit results are shown, some general information on the determination procedure has to be provided. The fits are performed with the LuminosityFit software using an extended binned log-likelihood estimator. With the typical data sample size of 10 6 events and a 2 D histogram binning of roughly 300 in each dimension a binned estimator is favored.
It was discovered that fits with a chi-square estimator give a systematic error on the luminosity in the order of 0 . 1 %. The reason for this is the assumption of a normal distributed bin content, which is not well enough satisfied for the used sample sizes and poisson statistics is preferable [ 110 ]. This systematic error mainly effects the normalization constant, but for the luminosity determination this is precisely the crucial parameter. A complete description of the likelihood estimator is given in section A. 1 .
When using a binned estimator it is important to compare the bin content with the integral of the model within the bin boundaries. This is in general a quite computation expensive calculation, especially if the model changes with the fit parameters. In the limit of fine binnings the function can be regarded as constant within the boundaries of a single bin and a single function evaluation normalized to the area of bin provides an accurate value for the integral. The two dimensional integrals for the luminosity fit are calculated by evaluating the model on a 3 × 3 grid within each bin, giving the necessary precision without large speed penalties. These integrals are cached and the luminosity fit model is now discretized according to the histogram of the data.

For the PANDA experiment, luminosity is determined by measuring the rate of antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering, a reference process with a well-understood physical cross section [4]. While the theoretical framework for this reference channel is firmly established, its experimental realization faces severe challenges. Unlike standard collider experiments with highly focused interaction points (IP), PANDA operates with a fixed-target setup using a Cluster-Jet target. The intense hydrogen jet causes the evaporation of hydrogen into the surrounding beam pipe which is called the residual gas or Restgas distribution. Interactions between the antiproton beam and the Restgas create continuously distributed interaction vertices along the beam axis [5]. This phenomenon results in a complex, extended target profile that deviates significantly from an ideal point-like target. Previous reconstruction algorithms, which naively approximate the IP as an extended point at the coordinate origin [6, 7], are fundamentally insufficient for this complex geometric situation. Neglecting the extensive spread of the target profiles leads to severe systematic biases in the luminosity determination, ultimately limiting the achievable precision of cross section measurements and resonance scans.
2
Motivation
This thesis addresses these critical challenges by developing a comprehensive, datadriven methodology that transforms the Restgas distribution from an unknown, limiting background contribution into a precisely monitored and continuously measurable observable. Central to this approach is the refinement of the software framework to explicitly account for the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap through the introduction of an 'Effective Acceptance Map'. To constrain the dominant systematic uncertainties associated with the Restgas density profile, this work evaluates a hardware-driven solution: upgrading the PANDA Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with state-of-the-art High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS). Leveraging the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS alongside a specialized off-IP reconstruction chain, this thesis establishes the feasibility of extracting the longitudinal Restgas distribution directly from tracking data. By integrating this measured profile back into the luminosity determination, the systematic uncertainty is successfully suppressed to better than 0 . 5%. Ultimately, this research provides the robust luminosity determination essential for fulfilling the high-precision physics goals of the PANDA experiment, ensuring that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum and explore the fundamental nature of the strong interaction.

3.1 The Concept of Luminosity
In high-energy physics experiments, the Luminosity ( ℒ ) is the fundamental parameter that relates the physical cross section ( 𝜎 ) of a specific reaction to the experimentally observed interaction rate ( 𝑅 ). It serves as the absolute overall normalization factor for virtually all physics analyses.
The instantaneous luminosity represents the intensity of the particle collisions, quantified as the number of interactions per unit area per unit time. For a fixed-target experimental setup like PANDA, the luminosity is determined by the specific beam and target parameters. It is defined as [2]:
where 𝑓 is the revolution frequency of the beam in the storage ring, 𝑛 𝑏 is the number of circulating bunches, 𝑁 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 is the number of particles per bunch, and 𝜌 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡 is the areal density of the target (number of target atoms per unit area). Consequently, the total interaction rate for a process is simply given by the relation 𝑅 = ℒ · 𝜎 𝑡𝑜𝑡 .
3.2 Motivation for Precise Luminosity Determination
The primary objective of the PANDA experiment is to study the strong interaction in the transitional region between perturbative and non-perturbative QCD. This involves high-precision spectroscopy of charmonium and open-charm states, alongside searches for exotic hadrons such as glueballs and hybrids. To successfully accomplish these physics goals, a precise determination of the luminosity is mandatory.

Summary and Outlook
The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) represents the future precision frontier of hadron physics, addressing fundamental questions regarding the strong interaction, including the search for gluonic excitations, the spectroscopy of charmonium states, and the investigation of nucleon structure. A prerequisite for fully exploiting this discovery potential-particularly for the measurement of absolute cross-sections and the scanning of narrow resonance lineshapes-is the precise determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While the primary luminosity measurement relies on the detection of antiproton-proton elastic scattering in the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference region, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixed-target setup introduce significant challenges that render conventional point-source approximations insufficient. Specifically, the interaction of the antiproton beam with the Restgas background distributed along the beam pipe creates a non-localized background source which, if not correctly modeled, fundamentally limits the attainable experimental precision.
To overcome these limitations, this thesis established a comprehensive methodology that transforms the handling of the extended interaction region from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. Central to this approach was the refinement of the object-oriented software framework LuminosityFit , which implements a rigorous convolution model combining the theoretical differential cross-section with the detector's resolution and geometric acceptance. By incorporating a Dual Parton Model (DPM) to accurately describe the hadronic amplitude and introducing the concept of an 'Effective Acceptance Map', the framework successfully integrates the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap into the fitting procedure. Extensive validation studies demonstrated that this algorithmic approach robustly decouples the luminosity signal from background contributions induced by beam systematics, effectively correcting for beam tilts, transverse offsets, and statistical divergence to recover the input luminosity with a relative statistical precision of better than 0.5%. However, sensitivity analysis revealed a critical dependency: the accuracy of the extraction is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. A deviation of 10% in the assumed Restgas model was shown to induce a systematic luminosity bias of approximately 3.4%, a magnitude that exceeds the stringent precision requirements necessary for the PANDA physics program.
To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

IP Alignment and Coordinate Transformation
A critical pre-processing step implemented in the framework is the alignment of the coordinate system. The standard laboratory frame assumes the interaction point is at (0 , 0 , 0). However, real beam operations imply a transverse offset ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ).
The framework utilizes the full 3D tracking information available after the backpropagation step to determine this offset geometrically. This results in a distribution of interaction vertices in the transverse plane. The arithmetic mean of these POCA coordinates is identified as the measurement of the mean interaction point ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0). This virtually shifts the detector system such that the interaction point coincides with the origin, restoring the azimuthal symmetry required for the 2D luminosity fit model.

The raw angular distribution measured by the LMD differs from the theoretical cross-section due to two distinct instrumental effects: the limited geometrical acceptance and the finite angular resolution. In the LuminosityFit framework, these effects are decoupled and treated sequentially using a forward-folding approach.

Compared to the point-source acceptance, the effective acceptance exhibits significant deviations. The point-source acceptance exhibits sharp boundaries and distinct efficiency drops corresponding to the gaps between sensor modules. This reflects the precise geometric projection of the detector as seen from the fixed center (0 , 0 , 0). In contrast, the effective acceptance necessary for the Restgas distribution displays significantly softer gradients. As the Restgas events originate from a range of 𝑧 positions, the projection of the sensor edges onto the angular plane ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) shifts continuously. Handling of Spatial Vertex Cuts
79
( 𝑥 𝑣𝑡𝑥 , 𝑦 𝑣𝑡𝑥 , 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 ) is essential for two primary reasons. First it isolates the core physics region by restricting the analysis to the 'Region of Physical Interest' where the beam-target overlap is maximal. Second, it provides robust background suppression by removing outliers and secondary interactions occurring far upstream or downstream or primary interactions outside the beam pipe.
The LuminosityFit framework supports the determination of the luminosity within any user-defined spatial range. However, applying geometric cuts on the experimental data fundamentally alters the reconstruction efficiency. If simple cuts are applied to the data but ignored in the fit model, the loss of signal events would be misinterpreted as a lower luminosity.
To ensure consistency, the framework introduces the concept of a Cut-Dependent Effective Acceptance Map. When a spatial cut condition Ω 𝑐𝑢𝑡 (e.g., | 𝑥 𝑣𝑡𝑥 , 𝑦 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 0 . 5 cm and | 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 1 cm) is applied to the data, the effective acceptance map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 is replaced by a modified map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑐𝑢𝑡 .
The modified acceptance map is derived from the same high-statistics Monte Carlo simulations as described for the determination of the effective acceptance map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 , but with the cut condition applied to the reconstructed MC events. The effictive acceptance map is defined as the ratio of the number of reconstructed events surviving the cut ( 𝑁 𝑐𝑢𝑡 𝑟𝑒𝑐 ) to the total number of generated events ( 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 ):
Here, 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) represents events generated in the whole angular phase space, reflecting the full physical process (e.g., the complete extended target density profile including Restgas background). 𝑁 𝑐𝑢𝑡 𝑟𝑒𝑐 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) is counted only by those MC tracks that are successfully reconstructed and whose back-propagated vertex falls within the defined cut limits.
By using 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑐𝑢𝑡 in the fit function:
the model correctly predicts the reduced event rate expected inside the cut region. Since the effective acceptance map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑐𝑢𝑡 implicitly includes the survival probability of the signal under the cut, the fitted parameter ℒ 𝑖𝑛𝑡 correctly recovers the total integrated luminosity of the experiment, compensating for the signal fraction removed by the cuts. This feature allows for robust stability checks, where the luminosity is determined under varying cut conditions (e.g., varying the 𝑧 -window) to verify the systematic stability of the measurement. Table 4.1 presents two representative vertex-cut scenarios at a beam momentum of 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , demonstrating the consistent recovery of the integrated luminosity. If the baseline effective acceptance map ( 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 ) is naively utilized, applying a tight spatial window ( | 𝑥 𝑣𝑡𝑥 , 𝑦 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 0 . 1 cm , | 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 0 . 3 cm) induces an artificial luminosity deviation exceeding 85%. Similarly, a looser window ( | 𝑥 𝑣𝑡𝑥 , 𝑦 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 0 . 5 cm , | 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 | < 1 . 0 cm) still yields a significant deviation of over 35%. However, these massive deviations completely vanish once the acceptance map is appropriately updated to incorporate the specific vertex cut conditions ( 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑐𝑢𝑡 ).

For a correct description one relies on the information of these two distributions, either from simulations or measurements. For the accelerator beam position a normal distribution in the xy plane is used. Estimations on the accelerator beam parameters are summarized in tables 2 and 3 . For the target beams there are two possible systems, the cluster jet target and pellet target. As the former will be used in the beginning of the ¯ PANDA runtime and measurements for the target beam distribution exist, this system was chosen in this study. The target hydrogen clusters follow the distribution given in equation 6 , with a slightly elongated shape in the z direction, while newest measurements even suggest a wider gaussian distribution[ 112 ]. Because the antiproton beam is costly to create and high reaction rates are desired, the target beam is usually broadened in the xy plane to have a good overlap with the antiproton beam. Therefore the dimensions of the IP distribution in the x and y direction are dictated by the size of the more narrow accelerator beam when performing the overlap. Hence a normal distribution for x and y with widths of σ x = σ y = 0 . 8 mm is used. Along the beam direction the distribution is dominated by the target beam profile and would be described best by equation 6 . However for reasons of simplicity a gaussian distribution with a similar width was used instead. The 2σ interval of the normal distribution should roughly equal the 13 . 1 mm size in z direction, therefore 4σ z ≈ 13 . 1 mm → σ z = 3 . 5 mm .
