Master Macros
=============

Introduction
------------

The master macros are the standard simulation and reconstruction macros of PandaRoot. 
They use the :ref:`MasterTasks` to have the most recent default settings for the detector simulation.

Running
-------

The typical sequence of macros is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- full_complete.C - Digitization, tracking and PID in one go
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

A sequence which expands the digi, reco and pid ito separate steps is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- digi_complete.C - Detector response simulation and local reconstruction
- reco_complete.C - Tracking
- pid_complete.C - Combine tracks with PID information
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

Common User Settings
--------------------

It is encouraged that you copy the macros to a location of your choice and work from there. 
For your own analysis you have to modify the ``sim_complete.C`` macro to set the proper event generation. EvtGen mostly serves for signal events, FTF for continuum background, while the BoxGenerator is there for detector studies.
Also you have to write your own analysis. 
The ``ana_complete.C`` macro may serve as a starting point. Also the tutorial section holds many examples to draw from.

The options available in the Master Tasks can be found at :ref:`MasterTasks`.

Typically the macro flow may look like this:

.. code-block:: bash

  nEvents=1000
  geant="TGeant4"
  beammom=6.231553
  prefix="../data/myAwesomeChannel"
  options="multikalman"
  
  root -l -b q sim_complete\($nEvents,\"$geant\",$beammom,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)
  root -l -b q full_complete\($nEvents,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)
  root -l -b q ana_complete\($nEvents,\"$prefix\",\"$options\"\)

(Virtual Monte-Carlo [60]), ROOT (Plotting, ﬁtting, graphics etc. [61]), Pythia [62]
and auxiliary tools
• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

7.3 Efficiency Analysis and Correction
The strategy described in the previous sections successfully reconstructed the IP of the single event, but the measured spectrum does not tell about the true physical density of the Restgas background. Due to the limited geometrical acceptance of the tracking system and the kinematic cuts applied during event selection, the detection probability varies significantly depending on the IP where the event originates. To extract the intrinsic Restgas profile 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) from the raw reconstructed data, an efficiency correction must be applied.
Before establishing the correction function, it is essential to determine the necessary dimensionality of the efficiency map. Specifically, we must ascertain whether the detection efficiency 𝜀 exhibits a significant dependence on the transverse and longitudinal coordinates ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), which would necessitate a complex 3D correction map 𝜀 ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), or if a simplified 1D curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) or even a constant 𝜀 0 suffices for the required precision.
To answer this question, a systematic simulation study was performed using the DPM generator to scan the interaction volume. The study covered a longitudinal range from 𝑧 = -10 cm to 𝑧 = +10cm with a step size of 2 . 5 cm. At each fixed longitudinal node, the efficiency was evaluated at various transverse offsets, covering 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ {± 0 . 1 , ± 0 . 2 , ± 0 . 3 , ± 0 . 5 , ± 0 . 8 } cm. This grid was designed to fully encompass the region of interest for beam-target and beam-Restgas interactions.

Chapter7
Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
The studies in Section 5.4 have clearly demonstrated the necessity of a precise measurement of the target distribution along the beam axis. Furthermore, the simulation studies in Section 6.3 have established that the upgraded MVD with HV-MAPS technology provides the necessary hardware performance, specifically the excellent spatial resolution and low material budget, to resolve the longitudinal distribution of Restgas background. However, the hardware upgrade alone is insufficient to extract the Restgas profile with the precision required for luminosity determination. To achieve this, the precise measurement of the longitudinal target profile will be performed specifically utilizing antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering events, which serve as a high-statistics and kinematically well-understood reference channel.
A fundamental challenge lies in the event reconstruction algorithms. The standard reconstruction chain in the PandaRoot framework is primarily optimized for physics channels originating from the nominal IP at (0 , 0 , 0). Beam-Restgas interactions, however, are distributed along the entire beam axis, often extending centimeters or decimeters away from the IP. Applying standard tracking and particle identification (PID) routines to these displaced vertices introduces systematic biases, as track parameters and error matrices are typically propagated to the origin rather than the true interaction vertex. To overcome this limitation, a dedicated reconstruction algorithm tailored for shifted IP scenarios is essential. This algorithm must accurately account for the spatial distribution of the beam-Restgas interactions, ensuring that track fitting and vertex reconstruction are performed with respect to the actual interaction points rather than the nominal IP.

Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

## 1. Physics goal

PANDA determines luminosity from a reference reaction with a known cross section, primarily elastic antiproton-proton scattering. In the fixed-target geometry, hydrogen from the cluster-jet target and residual gas in the beam pipe form an interaction region that is extended along the beam axis.

The measured vertex spectrum is therefore not simply the physical gas-density profile. It is modified by:

- detector acceptance;
- tracking and PID efficiency;
- displaced-vertex reconstruction efficiency;
- position-dependent resolution and migration between longitudinal bins;
- event-selection cuts.

The purpose of this repository is to reconstruct the interaction vertex for off-IP events and recover the underlying Restgas profile through a profile-dependent efficiency correction.

The final quantity of interest is the longitudinal interaction-density shape

```math
\rho_{\mathrm{gas}}(z),
```

or, in binned form, the generated number of interactions $N_{\mathrm{true},i}$ in each longitudinal bin.

Spatial Density Distribution
The following study is based on the Cluster Jet Target developed by Münster Group, which is currently the default target option for PANDA. The PANDA Cluster Jet Target generates a directed stream of hydrogen clusters by expanding pre-cooled hydrogen gas through a fine Laval nozzle into the vacuum. The expansion creates a core jet of solidified hydrogen clusters. A system of skimmers and collimators is employed to geometrically define this beam, removing the majority of the uncondensed gas. Ideally, this results in a well-defined target density profile 𝜌 𝑗𝑒𝑡 with a transverse diameter of few millimeters to centimeters at the interaction point ( 𝑧 = 0). Due to the constant flow of the jet, the time-averaged density 𝜌 𝑗𝑒𝑡 ( 𝑧 ) is modeled as a flat distribution in the longitudinal direction, with a width 𝜎 𝑗𝑒𝑡 determined by the jet's geometrical intersection with the beam ( 𝜎 𝑗𝑒𝑡 = 2cm) [138].
However, despite the skimmers, a fraction of the hydrogen gas inevitably enters the scattering chamber. This arises from two mechanisms:
Gas Halo: Imperfect separation of the clusters from the carrier gas leads to a diffuse 'curtain' of hydrogen molecules accompanying the main jet.
Evaporation and Scattering: Clusters interacting with the beam pipe edges or evaporating during flight contribute to a continuous gas load.
The shape of the residual gas distribution 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) is governed by the dynamic equilibrium between the gas load from the target and the effective pumping speed at the interaction region. Due to the limited conductance of the narrow beam pipe and the placement of the vacuum pumps the gas density is not uniform.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

For the PANDA experiment, luminosity is determined by measuring the rate of antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering, a reference process with a well-understood physical cross section [4]. While the theoretical framework for this reference channel is firmly established, its experimental realization faces severe challenges. Unlike standard collider experiments with highly focused interaction points (IP), PANDA operates with a fixed-target setup using a Cluster-Jet target. The intense hydrogen jet causes the evaporation of hydrogen into the surrounding beam pipe which is called the residual gas or Restgas distribution. Interactions between the antiproton beam and the Restgas create continuously distributed interaction vertices along the beam axis [5]. This phenomenon results in a complex, extended target profile that deviates significantly from an ideal point-like target. Previous reconstruction algorithms, which naively approximate the IP as an extended point at the coordinate origin [6, 7], are fundamentally insufficient for this complex geometric situation. Neglecting the extensive spread of the target profiles leads to severe systematic biases in the luminosity determination, ultimately limiting the achievable precision of cross section measurements and resonance scans.
2
Motivation
This thesis addresses these critical challenges by developing a comprehensive, datadriven methodology that transforms the Restgas distribution from an unknown, limiting background contribution into a precisely monitored and continuously measurable observable. Central to this approach is the refinement of the software framework to explicitly account for the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap through the introduction of an 'Effective Acceptance Map'. To constrain the dominant systematic uncertainties associated with the Restgas density profile, this work evaluates a hardware-driven solution: upgrading the PANDA Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with state-of-the-art High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS). Leveraging the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS alongside a specialized off-IP reconstruction chain, this thesis establishes the feasibility of extracting the longitudinal Restgas distribution directly from tracking data. By integrating this measured profile back into the luminosity determination, the systematic uncertainty is successfully suppressed to better than 0 . 5%. Ultimately, this research provides the robust luminosity determination essential for fulfilling the high-precision physics goals of the PANDA experiment, ensuring that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum and explore the fundamental nature of the strong interaction.

Integration with MVD and GEM (Global Tracking)
The output of the combined Apollonius and Pz Finder stages is a track seed based solely on STT information. While this seed is highly effective for identifying displaced tracks, it does not yet provide the precision required for accurate vertex reconstruction. The full integration of information from all tracking sub-detectors is therefore performed in the final Kalman filtering stage.
The Apollonius algorithm supplies an initial track candidate derived from STT isochrones, which defines a preliminary trajectory but does not include the highprecision measurements from the silicon-based detectors. These track candidates are subsequently processed by the KalmanFit using the GenFit framework, which applies a statistically rigorous Kalman filter to combine measurements from different detector systems. During this procedure, the STT-based helix is extrapolated inward toward the MVD volume, where compatible pixel or strip hits are searched for and, if found, incorporated into the track. This inward propagation significantly improves the resolution of the impact parameters 𝑑 0 and 𝑧 0 and is crucial for precisely locating the interaction vertex. In parallel, the track is extrapolated outward to the GEM stations, where additional measurements refine the momentum determination, particularly for forward-going particles, leading to an improved relative momentum resolution 𝑑𝑝/𝑝 .
As a result, the final reconstructed tracks coherently combine information from all tracking subsystems-MVD, STT, and GEM-leveraging the large acceptance and pattern recognition capability of the STT together with the superior spatial resolution of the MVD and GEM to achieve precise vertex and momentum reconstruction.
PID Step
The accurate determination of particle kinematics relies not only on precise track fitting but also on the correct association of reconstructed tracks with their physical interaction vertex during the PID step. Track candidates produced by the track finder are represented as infinite helices extending throughout the detector volume. Consequently, a crucial task of the PID step is the determination of the true physical origin of these trajectories, in order to effectively anchor and terminate them at their source. Without a well-defined starting point, essential kinematic quantities-most notably the momentum vector and the path length required for energy-loss corrections-cannot be uniquely or reliably determined.
This issue becomes particularly severe in the presence of Restgas background, where interactions occur at arbitrary locations along and within the beam pipe rather than being confined to the nominal target region. Under these conditions, the IP determination approach in the PID step must be reconsidered.
Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.

While the beam properties discussed in the previous chapter primarily affect the angular resolution, the properties of the target introduce a spatial complexity that fundamentally challenges the point-like interaction assumption. In the PANDA fixedtarget setup, the interaction region is not confined to a dimensionless point but follows the density distribution of the gas molecules along the beam axis.
Origin of the Restgas
The primary interaction region in PANDA is a stream of frozen hydrogen pellets or a cluster jet, intersecting the antiproton beam at the nominal interaction point (IP, 𝑧 = 0). Ideally, the scattering process occurs exclusively within the geometric overlap of the beam and this target stream.
However, the injection of target material into the beam pipe inherently degrades the local vacuum quality. Despite the high-capacity pumping system, a fraction of the hydrogen target evaporates or scatters out of the main stream, creating a cloud of so-called Restgas. This gas accumulates within the scattering chamber and diffuses along the beam pipe until it is removed by the nearest vacuum pumps. Figure 4.1 shows the vacuum pump locations at PANDA close to the interaction point.
Consequently, the antiproton beam interacts not only with the dense target but also with this low-density Restgas. Crucially, these Beam-Restgas interactions (¯ 𝑝𝑝 → ¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) are kinematically indistinguishable from the desired signal Beam-Target interactions, as they share the exact same final state particles and kinematics. While the signal events are highly localized at the nominal interaction point ( 𝑧 ≈ 0), the Restgas background events are continuously distributed along the entire 𝑧 -axis of the beam pipe.

Summary and Outlook
The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) represents the future precision frontier of hadron physics, addressing fundamental questions regarding the strong interaction, including the search for gluonic excitations, the spectroscopy of charmonium states, and the investigation of nucleon structure. A prerequisite for fully exploiting this discovery potential-particularly for the measurement of absolute cross-sections and the scanning of narrow resonance lineshapes-is the precise determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While the primary luminosity measurement relies on the detection of antiproton-proton elastic scattering in the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference region, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixed-target setup introduce significant challenges that render conventional point-source approximations insufficient. Specifically, the interaction of the antiproton beam with the Restgas background distributed along the beam pipe creates a non-localized background source which, if not correctly modeled, fundamentally limits the attainable experimental precision.
To overcome these limitations, this thesis established a comprehensive methodology that transforms the handling of the extended interaction region from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. Central to this approach was the refinement of the object-oriented software framework LuminosityFit , which implements a rigorous convolution model combining the theoretical differential cross-section with the detector's resolution and geometric acceptance. By incorporating a Dual Parton Model (DPM) to accurately describe the hadronic amplitude and introducing the concept of an 'Effective Acceptance Map', the framework successfully integrates the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap into the fitting procedure. Extensive validation studies demonstrated that this algorithmic approach robustly decouples the luminosity signal from background contributions induced by beam systematics, effectively correcting for beam tilts, transverse offsets, and statistical divergence to recover the input luminosity with a relative statistical precision of better than 0.5%. However, sensitivity analysis revealed a critical dependency: the accuracy of the extraction is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. A deviation of 10% in the assumed Restgas model was shown to induce a systematic luminosity bias of approximately 3.4%, a magnitude that exceeds the stringent precision requirements necessary for the PANDA physics program.
To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

# RestgasDetermination

A PandaRoot-based research branch for reconstructing and correcting the longitudinal residual-gas (“Restgas”) interaction profile in the PANDA target region.

This repository is based on the PandaRoot `oct19` tag. The Restgas-specific development starts after commit `ef9a564`. The principal analysis code is located in [`macro/target`](macro/target). This document describes the current `oct19` workflow, including the event-by-event POCA hand-off, configurable beam momentum and Restgas profile, and profile-dependent efficiency correction.

> **Scope and maturity**
>
> The current repository is a **Monte Carlo research implementation used for the studies in Chapters 7 and 8 of the associated thesis**. It contains the main ingredients of the Restgas-determination method, including distributed target generation, displaced-track reconstruction, POCA-based back-propagation, vertex reconstruction, and profile-dependent efficiency correction.
>
> The analysis and correction macros are designed primarily for Monte Carlo closure, efficiency, and systematic studies corresponding to the thesis workflow.

raw.title: 1. Physics goal
raw.text:
## 1. Physics goal

PANDA determines luminosity from a reference reaction with a known cross section, primarily elastic antiproton-proton scattering. In the fixed-target geometry, hydrogen from the cluster-jet target and residual gas in the beam pipe form an interaction region that is extended along the beam axis.

The measured vertex spectrum is therefore not simply the physical gas-density profile. It is modified by:

- detector acceptance;
- tracking and PID efficiency;
- displaced-vertex reconstruction efficiency;
- position-dependent resolution and migration between longitudinal bins;
- event-selection cuts.

The purpose of this repository is to reconstruct the interaction vertex for off-IP events and recover the underlying Restgas profile through a profile-dependent efficiency correction.

The final quantity of interest is the longitudinal interaction-density shape

```math
\rho_{\mathrm{gas}}(z),
```

or, in binned form, the generated number of interactions $N_{\mathrm{true},i}$ in each longitudinal bin.

The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

Summary and Outlook
The culmination of this work is the integration of the measured Restgas profile back into the luminosity determination chain, establishing a self-consistent analysis cycle. Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the target profile with Restgas background is successfully reconstructed without the reliance on the initial model. The reconstructed profile is then used to generate an 'Effective Acceptance Map' for the luminosity fit, effectively suppressing the systematic uncertainty associated with the target profile with Restgas background to better than 0.5%. By proving that the Restgas distribution can be precisely reconstructed and accounted for, this research ensures that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the PANDA experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum, thereby fulfilling the rigorous demands of next-generation hadron physics.

7.3 Efficiency Analysis and Correction
The strategy described in the previous sections successfully reconstructed the IP of the single event, but the measured spectrum does not tell about the true physical density of the Restgas background. Due to the limited geometrical acceptance of the tracking system and the kinematic cuts applied during event selection, the detection probability varies significantly depending on the IP where the event originates. To extract the intrinsic Restgas profile 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) from the raw reconstructed data, an efficiency correction must be applied.
Before establishing the correction function, it is essential to determine the necessary dimensionality of the efficiency map. Specifically, we must ascertain whether the detection efficiency 𝜀 exhibits a significant dependence on the transverse and longitudinal coordinates ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), which would necessitate a complex 3D correction map 𝜀 ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), or if a simplified 1D curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) or even a constant 𝜀 0 suffices for the required precision.
To answer this question, a systematic simulation study was performed using the DPM generator to scan the interaction volume. The study covered a longitudinal range from 𝑧 = -10 cm to 𝑧 = +10cm with a step size of 2 . 5 cm. At each fixed longitudinal node, the efficiency was evaluated at various transverse offsets, covering 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ {± 0 . 1 , ± 0 . 2 , ± 0 . 3 , ± 0 . 5 , ± 0 . 8 } cm. This grid was designed to fully encompass the region of interest for beam-target and beam-Restgas interactions.

Efficiency Analysis and Correction
131
The results of this dependency study are summarized in Figure 7.6. The analysis reveals a dramatic variation in efficiency along the beam axis ( 𝑧 ). As the interaction point shifts away from the detector center, the efficiency drops precipitously from a maximum of ∼ 81% at 𝑧 = 0cm to approximately 6% at the downstream edge 𝑧 = 10cm, primarily due to the acceptance coverage of the PANDA Target Spectrometer. In strong contrast, the efficiency remains remarkably stable with respect to transverse displacements. Within the central core region ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 0 . 5 cm), the variation in efficiency is negligible. Considering that the transverse profile of the real beam-Restgas interaction is tightly constrained by the beam emittance (typically well within the ± 0 . 5 cm window), the transverse efficiency uniformity holds true for the experimental conditions.
Consequently, this study concludes that the transverse dependence can be safely neglected. A 1D longitudinal efficiency curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) provides a sufficient and robust model for the correction of the reconstructed data. This finding allows for the precise recovery of the Restgas distribution by simply weighting the reconstructed 𝑧 -spectrum by the inverse of the z-dependent efficiency, significantly simplifying the analysis framework without compromising physical accuracy.

## 2. Method overview

The complete physics method consists of five stages:

1. **Generate or read an extended target profile.**
2. **Reconstruct tracks without imposing the nominal interaction point.**
3. **Estimate the interaction vertex from the track-pair POCA.**
4. **Back-propagate tracks to that vertex and perform the final vertex fit.**
5. **Correct the reconstructed $z$ distribution with a profile-dependent efficiency map.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input target / Restgas profile rho_in(z)"]
    B["Simulation and digitization"]
    C["Apollonius displaced-track finding"]
    D["Skewed-STT z reconstruction and Kalman fit"]
    E["Initial PID without back-propagation"]
    F["p-pbar POCA vertex estimate"]
    G["Second PID with back-propagation to POCA"]
    H["Final event vertex fit"]
    I["Raw reconstructed z spectrum"]
    J["Profile-dependent MC efficiency epsilon_reco(z)"]
    K["Corrected Restgas profile"]
    L["Optional iteration with corrected profile"]

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H --> I
    A --> J
    B --> J
    I --> K
    J --> K
    K --> L --> J
```

The thesis-level target workflow is **event-by-event**:

```text
raw hits
  -> Apollonius track candidates
  -> Kalman-fitted tracks
  -> PID without back-propagation
  -> event POCA
  -> reuse the original Kalman tracks
  -> PID with back-propagation to the event POCA
  -> final vertex fit
  -> reconstructed Restgas profile
```

The repository implements this event-by-event chain for both fixed-vertex and continuously distributed Restgas samples. It also provides an MC-truth control mode for closure studies.

Chapter8
Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

134

8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

Summary and Outlook
The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) represents the future precision frontier of hadron physics, addressing fundamental questions regarding the strong interaction, including the search for gluonic excitations, the spectroscopy of charmonium states, and the investigation of nucleon structure. A prerequisite for fully exploiting this discovery potential-particularly for the measurement of absolute cross-sections and the scanning of narrow resonance lineshapes-is the precise determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While the primary luminosity measurement relies on the detection of antiproton-proton elastic scattering in the Coulomb-Nuclear Interference region, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixed-target setup introduce significant challenges that render conventional point-source approximations insufficient. Specifically, the interaction of the antiproton beam with the Restgas background distributed along the beam pipe creates a non-localized background source which, if not correctly modeled, fundamentally limits the attainable experimental precision.
To overcome these limitations, this thesis established a comprehensive methodology that transforms the handling of the extended interaction region from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. Central to this approach was the refinement of the object-oriented software framework LuminosityFit , which implements a rigorous convolution model combining the theoretical differential cross-section with the detector's resolution and geometric acceptance. By incorporating a Dual Parton Model (DPM) to accurately describe the hadronic amplitude and introducing the concept of an 'Effective Acceptance Map', the framework successfully integrates the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap into the fitting procedure. Extensive validation studies demonstrated that this algorithmic approach robustly decouples the luminosity signal from background contributions induced by beam systematics, effectively correcting for beam tilts, transverse offsets, and statistical divergence to recover the input luminosity with a relative statistical precision of better than 0.5%. However, sensitivity analysis revealed a critical dependency: the accuracy of the extraction is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. A deviation of 10% in the assumed Restgas model was shown to induce a systematic luminosity bias of approximately 3.4%, a magnitude that exceeds the stringent precision requirements necessary for the PANDA physics program.
To constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, the investigation extended beyond software algorithms to evaluate the feasibility of a hardware-driven solution utilizing the tracking system. The study proposed the upgrade of the Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), leveraging technology originally developed for the Luminosity Detector itself. It was demonstrated that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS, thinned to just 50 𝜇 m, minimizes the multiple Coulomb scattering that typically degrades tracking performance at low momenta. Coupled with a fine pixel pitch of 80 × 80 𝜇 m 2 , this hardware configuration achieves a longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m, providing the necessary sensitivity to resolve the Restgas distribution which is inaccessible to the Luminosity Detector alone. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized reconstruction chain was implemented, utilizing the Apollonius triplet finder for off-IP tracking and a 'POCA-to-Point' back-propagation algorithm. This strategy optimized the reconstruction efficiency for events originating away from the nominal interaction point, allowing for the recovery of the physical density profile via a robust one-dimensional efficiency correction.

Abstract
Understanding the dynamics of the strong interaction and the nature of exotic hadronic matter represents a fundamental frontier in modern physics. The PANDA experiment at the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) is designed to explore this regime with unprecedented precision. However, a strict prerequisite for achieving its primary physics goals, particularly the absolute cross section measurements and high-precision resonance energy scans, is the highly accurate determination of the time-integrated luminosity. While this primary measurement relies on antiproton-proton elastic scattering, the specific conditions of the PANDA fixedtarget setup introduce a critical challenge. The interaction of the antiproton beam with residual gas (Restgas) creates a continuously distributed background along the beam pipe. This complex, non-localized interaction region fundamentally breaks standard point-like approximations and severely limits the achievable experimental precision.
This thesis establishes a comprehensive, data-driven methodology that transforms this Restgas background distribution from a systematic liability into a precisely controlled observable. First, the software framework, LuminosityFit , was extended to handle the Restgas distribution during the luminosity determination process. However, the accuracy of the determination is strictly bound to the prior knowledge of the longitudinal Restgas density profile. To dynamically constrain this dominant systematic uncertainty, this work evaluates the upgrade of the PANDA Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HVMAPS). Simulations demonstrate that the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS (thinned to 50 𝜇 m) minimizes multiple scattering, achieving an exceptional longitudinal vertex resolution of approximately 20 𝜇 m. To fully exploit this hardware potential, a specialized off-IP reconstruction chain was developed to efficiently reconstruct highly displaced vertices originating from beam-Restgas interactions.
Ultimately, by integrating the experimentally measured Restgas profile back into the luminosity determination chain, the overall systematic uncertainty including the Restgas background is better than 0 . 5%. This research proves that the synergy of advanced fitting frameworks and high-precision HV-MAPS tracking provides a robust solution, ensuring that normalization uncertainties will not limit the PANDA experiment's capability to achieve its physics goals.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

Furthermore, the simulation studies in Section 6.3 have established that the upgraded MVD with HV-MAPS technology provides the necessary hardware performance, specifically the excellent spatial resolution and low material budget, to resolve the longitudinal distribution of Restgas background. However, the hardware upgrade alone is insufficient to extract the Restgas profile with the precision required for luminosity determination. To achieve this, the precise measurement of the longitudinal target profile will be performed specifically utilizing antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering events, which serve as a high-statistics and kinematically well-understood reference channel.
A fundamental challenge lies in the event reconstruction algorithms. The standard reconstruction chain in the PandaRoot framework is primarily optimized for physics channels originating from the nominal IP at (0 , 0 , 0). Beam-Restgas interactions, however, are distributed along the entire beam axis, often extending centimeters or decimeters away from the IP. Applying standard tracking and particle identification (PID) routines to these displaced vertices introduces systematic biases, as track parameters and error matrices are typically propagated to the origin rather than the true interaction vertex. To overcome this limitation, a dedicated reconstruction algorithm tailored for shifted IP scenarios is essential. This algorithm must accurately account for the spatial distribution of the beam-Restgas interactions, ensuring that track fitting and vertex reconstruction are performed with respect to the actual interaction points rather than the nominal IP.
7.1 Reconstruction Strategy
The accurate reconstruction of the interaction vertex distribution of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events which also originate by interactions of beam particles with Restgas profiles necessitates specialized algorithms capable of handling displaced vertices.

The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. The superior vertexing resolution and reduced material budget of the sensors are critical factors that enable the effective determination of the Restgas distribution even for interactions significantly displaced from the nominal IP.
Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the systematic distortions caused by resolution smearing and initial model inaccuracies are rigorously suppressed. This method acts as a contracting map, converging to the true physical distribution and ensuring that the final result is independent of the initial simulation input provided by the Target Group. To quantify the stability of this approach, an iterative procedure was initialized with an extreme starting condition: a 40% overestimation of the Restgas distribution. As summarized in Table 9.1, the iterative procedure converges rapidly. Within merely three steps, the global deviation drops from 12 . 27% to 1 . 30%, and the deviation in the central region vanishes to -0 . 22%. Consequently, the precise density profile can be derived directly from the experimental data across the entire relevant domain, providing the reliable input essential for the absolute luminosity determination.
Finally, the determined Restgas profile was integrated back into the LuminosityFit framework to validate the complete analysis chain. The luminosity determination was performed at a beam momentum of 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , applying a cut within the analysis window ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 1 cm and | 𝑧 | < 5 cm). The relative deviation of the determined luminosity (Δ ℒ / ℒ ) is (0 . 05 ± 0 . 07)% with the reconstructed target profile with Restgas background. As presented in Table 9.2, this result is consistent with the ideal case where the target is treated as point-like and the efficiency correction is based on a point-like model, which yields a deviation of -0 . 036 ± 0 . 07% and also with the case where the target profile with Restgas background is well-known and totally the same as real data, which yields a deviation of 0 . 02 ± 0 . 08%. This results demonstrate that the synergy of high-precision tracking and advanced fitting algorithms transforms the Restgas background from a limiting systematic background into a precisely monitored observable, enabling a robust and accurate luminosity determination for the PANDA experiment.

8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

7.3 Efficiency Analysis and Correction
The strategy described in the previous sections successfully reconstructed the IP of the single event, but the measured spectrum does not tell about the true physical density of the Restgas background. Due to the limited geometrical acceptance of the tracking system and the kinematic cuts applied during event selection, the detection probability varies significantly depending on the IP where the event originates. To extract the intrinsic Restgas profile 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) from the raw reconstructed data, an efficiency correction must be applied.
Before establishing the correction function, it is essential to determine the necessary dimensionality of the efficiency map. Specifically, we must ascertain whether the detection efficiency 𝜀 exhibits a significant dependence on the transverse and longitudinal coordinates ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), which would necessitate a complex 3D correction map 𝜀 ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), or if a simplified 1D curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) or even a constant 𝜀 0 suffices for the required precision.
To answer this question, a systematic simulation study was performed using the DPM generator to scan the interaction volume. The study covered a longitudinal range from 𝑧 = -10 cm to 𝑧 = +10cm with a step size of 2 . 5 cm. At each fixed longitudinal node, the efficiency was evaluated at various transverse offsets, covering 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ {± 0 . 1 , ± 0 . 2 , ± 0 . 3 , ± 0 . 5 , ± 0 . 8 } cm. This grid was designed to fully encompass the region of interest for beam-target and beam-Restgas interactions.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

raw.text:
# ProcessTask

To be able to separate algorithm implementation from **FairRoot**s specific **Task** setup, a **Task-Process** split up was performed on the PANDA EMC simulation and reconstruction code. The goal was to reduce the dependency on **FairRoot** of our PandaRoot algorithms, such as clustering. This requires to separate data and parameter fetching, which are done using the **FairRoot** infrastructure, from the actual algorithm implementation. So far, data and parameter fetching as well as algorithm implementation was done within one **FairTask**-derived class. This is now separated into a **Task** (or ProcessHandler), just dealing with the fetching of parameters and data and passing that to a new type of class, the **Process**, which contains the algorithm implementation.

Each **Process** defines, which parameter it needs. The **Task**(/ProcessHandler) handling the **Process** fetches that parameterlist for each **Process** and stores this parameterlist in a **ParameterRegister**, which is a simple map mapping a parametername/key to a pointer to a **FairParSet**. How the **ParameterRegister** is populated with the appropriate **FairParSet** pointers is then defined in the **Task**(/ProcessHandler). This could be by just using the **FairRuntimeDb** or via **FairRuntimeDb-Server** and **MessageQueues**.

**Task**(/ProcessHandler) will also define a set of data containers they are going to fetch. The addresses/pointers of these data containers are then passed to the **Process** via a processing-stage specific data struct.

![PndProcessSetup](./PndProcessSetup.png)

The **Process**es are going to be executed in the order they were added to the **Task**(/ProcessHandler). This requires certain knowledge of the order in which **Process**es need to be placed by the user.

---

raw.text:
# ProcessTask

To be able to separate algorithm implementation from **FairRoot**s specific **Task** setup, a **Task-Process** split up was performed on the PANDA EMC simulation and reconstruction code. The goal was to reduce the dependency on **FairRoot** of our PandaRoot algorithms, such as clustering. This requires to separate data and parameter fetching, which are done using the **FairRoot** infrastructure, from the actual algorithm implementation. So far, data and parameter fetching as well as algorithm implementation was done within one **FairTask**-derived class. This is now separated into a **Task** (or ProcessHandler), just dealing with the fetching of parameters and data and passing that to a new type of class, the **Process**, which contains the algorithm implementation.

Each **Process** defines, which parameter it needs. The **Task**(/ProcessHandler) handling the **Process** fetches that parameterlist for each **Process** and stores this parameterlist in a **ParameterRegister**, which is a simple map mapping a parametername/key to a pointer to a **FairParSet**. How the **ParameterRegister** is populated with the appropriate **FairParSet** pointers is then defined in the **Task**(/ProcessHandler). This could be by just using the **FairRuntimeDb** or via **FairRuntimeDb-Server** and **MessageQueues**.

**Task**(/ProcessHandler) will also define a set of data containers they are going to fetch. The addresses/pointers of these data containers are then passed to the **Process** via a processing-stage specific data struct.

![PndProcessSetup](./PndProcessSetup.png)

The **Process**es are going to be executed in the order they were added to the **Task**(/ProcessHandler). This requires certain knowledge of the order in which **Process**es need to be placed by the user.

---
## Classes
- [PndParameterRegister](PndParameterRegister.h): Simple map mapping a parametername to a pointer to a **FairParSet**. Is passed from **PndProcessHandler** to **PndProcess** as indirection layer.

- [PndProcess](PndProcess.h): Base class for all algorithm implementations.
Offers functions to "Setup" the process at beginning of simulation/analysation: set data, "request" and set parameters as well as a TearDown function called once simulation/analysation has finished.
Else offers functions Pro/Post/Process() function. If in doubt only override Process().

- [PndProcessHandler](PndProcessHandler.h): Base class for all **PndProcess** using entities. User adds **PndProcess** to the **PndProcessHandler**, the **PndProcessHandler** takes care of propagation data addresses to the **PndProcess** via the **DataStruct** and adds the **PndProcess** ParameterRequest List to the **PndParameterRegister**. The filling/fetching of **PndParameterRegister** has to be implemented by derived class.

- [PndProcessTask](PndProcessTask.h): Derives from **FairTask** and **PndProcessHandler**. Implements FairRoot specific way of filling **PndParameterRegister** via **FairRuntimeDb**.
Derive from **PndProcessTask** to implement fetching of required data arrays via **PndContainer** or directly via **FairRootManager**.

Finally also the distributions in the other decay topology can be verified. For this data samples with a 1 --intermediate resonance, which then decays into the γπ 0 , were created. The cos ( θ γπ 0 γ ) distributions of the decay of the intermediate state are shown in figure 65 . Since this is also a spin 1 resonance, just like the mother state J/ψ , their distributions are also identical. Note that the distributions for the λ = 0 and | λ | = 1 case are swapped in comparison to the distributions of the J/ψ decay. The reason for this is, that the Wigner D functions are evaluated differently with the denoted λ variable for these two decays. In the J/ψ decay λ refers to the helicity of a decay product, in contrast to the decay of the intermediate state, where λ belongs to the decaying state itself. Therefore the λ variable swaps index positions in the Wigner D functions for these two different decays, which induces the interchange of the distributions. Also it should be noted that the λ = 0 case does not occur for a parity conserving decay, as the decay of the J/ψ into a π 0 and the ω with λ = 0 is forbidden. The agreement of the angular distributions with the theory is again perfect.
This perfect agreement was visible consistently, also for rather complex amplitudes of particles of spin 4 , which means that the implementation of the angular distributions for single decay channels is implemented correctly. Refer to appendix C. 2 for a complete listing of the angular distributions. There also the kinematic distributions in the opposing subsystems are shown, which cannot be calculated analytically and are in general nontrivial distributions with kinematic reflections from the intermediate state subsystem.
7 . 3 first validation with a simple model
As a next step in the validation process, input-output checks of the HelicityAmplitude module are performed. For this an amplitude model is constructed that is used for both the data generation and fitting with ComPWA. In this section a simple amplitude was created, using only the f 0 ( 2020 ) and the f 2 ( 1270 ) resonance. The choice of these specific f resonances is based on their strong presence in the BESIII data [ 120 ]. All possible helicities for the occuring states are used, except for the spin projection component of the J/ψ equal to zero, as noted above. In addition a coherently added background term, distributed uniformly in phase space, is introduced.

With respect to the statistical errors the mean values are in agreement with the generated parameters, implicating a high accuracy of the fit parameters. Just as in the previous validations, the error are marginally underestimated.
At this point the validation of the helicity formalism implementation in the ComPWA framework is declared as complete.
7 . 6 a first fit on the BESIII data
The BESIII dataset of the decay J/ψ → γπ 0 π 0 originates from the reference [ 51 , 120 ]. Also a corresponding phase space MC dataset for the efficiency correction is available. It should emphasized that the goal is not a full analysis of the data, but a first real data test case for the ComPWA helicity formalism implementation. In total the data contains 442562 events and the corresponding acceptance corrected phase space sample amounts to roughly 1 . 6 ∗ 10 6 events.
Figure 76 : Dalitz plot of the BESIII data of the reaction J/ψ → γπ 0 π 0 (left) and in logarithmic scale (right). The ω bands have been removed [ 120 ].
The Dalitz plot of the data is shown in figure 76 . Immediately noticeable is the strongest contribution in the π 0 π 0 mass combination at a squared mass of roughly 1 . 6 GeV 2 /c 4 . Comparing this with the previous Dalitz plots (see figure 72 ), the f 2 ( 1270 ) state can be foreshadowed. Both the mass and the spin 2 ( λ = 0 ) modulation, with peaks at the phase space boundaries and the slight bump in the center of the band, match the f 2 ( 1270 ) . Several other resonances in the squared mass range from 2 -5 GeV 2 /c 4 are also visible by eye. A relatively strong uniform spin 0 band is located at around 3 GeV 2 /c 4 . The broad band at 4 GeV 2 /c 4 shows higher spin modulations, thus one would naively suspect multiple intermediate states with interference. However for precise quantative statements a partial wave analysis is indispensable.
A helicity intensity was generated with ComPWA including all intermediate states as stated in the reference [ 120 , p. 109 ]. A first fit on the data was performed within the scope of the thesis. In total 48 parameters of the model were optimized by the minimizer. The parameters are again initialized randomly using the same intervals as for the validation tests shown in the previous sections. Generally a single fit is not sufficient to guarantee the finding of the global minimum. In the case of this first fit, the minimizer from the optimization library MINUIT 2 was able to find a valid minimum region and successfully stopped the gradient descent procedure. However to validate the minimium, and obtain a more precise location of the minimum with a symmetric error estimation of fit parameters, the Hesse algorithm is executed afterwards. This additional Hesse calculation failed, which could indicate that not the global minimum was found. Hence no particularly good description of the data is expected, and this result should be interpreted with care. The obtained fit parameters and the errors are listed in table 11 .

When using a binned estimator it is important to compare the bin content with the integral of the model within the bin boundaries. This is in general a quite computation expensive calculation, especially if the model changes with the fit parameters. In the limit of fine binnings the function can be regarded as constant within the boundaries of a single bin and a single function evaluation normalized to the area of bin provides an accurate value for the integral. The two dimensional integrals for the luminosity fit are calculated by evaluating the model on a 3 × 3 grid within each bin, giving the necessary precision without large speed penalties. These integrals are cached and the luminosity fit model is now discretized according to the histogram of the data.

CernVM-FS installation
¶
CernVM-FS was successfully installed on your Mac.cvmfs-config.cern.ch
There are only two steps necessary to access any repository:
Mount the CernVM-FS config repository:
• sudo mkdir -p /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
• sudo mount -t cvmfs /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
Mount a CernVM-FS repository using the following steps:
• sudo mkdir /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
• sudo mount -t cvmfs sft.cern.ch /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
Please note that from MacOS 10.15 Catalina is necessary to reboot your system after the installation in order to create the /cvmfs directory.
Enjoy!
Client configuration
¶
client
:
Install
cvmfs
using your distribution’s package manager.
Copy the
master public key
to
/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub
.
Place the repository-specific config file to
/etc/cvmfs/config.d/
. For GSI-internal repositories, use Stratum 0 (an HTTP proxy is usually used automatically on centrally managed GSI machines). For publicly reachable repositories, use Stratum 1.
Example for public repositories:
fairsoft.gsi.de.conf
:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
=
"http://cvmfs-s1.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY
=
"DIRECT"
CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY
=
"/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"
Example for GSI-internal repositories:
fairsoft.gsi.de.conf
:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
=
"http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY
=
"DIRECT"
CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY
=
"/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"
Instead of duplicating the repo name in the
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
, you can also use
@fqrn@
there like this:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/@fqrn@"
.
Mount the desired repository through any of the available mechanisms. Example for a systemd unit file
cvmfs-cvmfstest.gsi.de.mount
:
[
Unit
]
Description
=
Mount
/
cvmfs
/
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de
After
=
network
.
target
[
Mount
]
What
=
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de
Where
=/
cvmfs
/
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de

=
cvmfs
[
Install
]

=
multi
-
user
.

On OSX
¶
On Mac OS X, CernVM-FS is based on
macFUSE
. Note that as of macOS 11 Big Sur, kernel extensions need to be
enabled
to install macFUSE. Verify that fuse is available with
kextstat
|
grep -i fuse
Download the CernVM-FS client package
in
the terminal
in
order to avoid signature warnings

curl -o ~/Downloads/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg https://ecsft.cern.ch/dist/cvmfs/cvmfs-2.8.0/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg
Install the CernVM-FS package by opening the .pkg file and reboot. Future releases will provide a signed and notarized package.
Mount each time with
sudo mount -t cvmfs fairsoft.gsi.de /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de/
Mount via Docker Container
¶
The steps explained in the [previous section](#client-configuration) have been packaged into a docker image
rklasen/cvmfs
. Running a container from this image provides FairSoft/FairRoot via CVMFS on the host at
/cvmfs
:
docker run -d --name cvmfs --privileged --cap-add SYS_ADMIN --device /dev/fuse --volume /cvmfs:/cvmfs:shared rklasen/cvmfs
The container continues to run in background. Check after about a minute whether it works
ls /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de

Please note the

container that includes all that’s needed for PandaRoot

type
=

/mnt/work/PandaRoot --volume
=
"/tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix:rw"
--volume /cvmfs:/cvmfs:shared --env

"DISPLAY"

Nothing else is required, that’s already it. A detailed explanation is [
down below
].
PandaRoot in a Docker Container
¶
You can compile, install and run PandaRoot in a Docker container. The advantages are:
You don’t have to install all needed packages system-wide
You can use system versions that are incompatible with PandaRoot (either too old or too new)
You can keep multiple different PandaRoot versions side by side
And probably others.
What is or should be included
¶
Usually, a complete PandaRoot installation meant you have to download FairSoft, compile and install it, download FairRoot, compile and install it and download PandaRoot and compile it (and of course yous system needs to have the needed packages installed). But since FairSoft and FairRoot are being built at the GSI and made available via CVMFS mount, not all of these steps are required anymore.
Currently, these scenarios are considered (
see also these slides
):
All-inclusive package. That means FairSoft/FairRoot and PandaRoot are included and compiled in this image and it’s ready from the get-go.
Pros:
All inclusive, no internet connection is required to run.
Cons:
Large image size, PandaRoot code can’t be (easily) modified.
Everything except PandaRoot. This is an image that includes FairSoft/FairRoot and all necessary packages, but not the PandaRoot Code. The PandaRoot code must be present on the host system and passed to the container, where it can be compiled and run.
Pros:
Edit PandaRoot code on host with favorite IDE, easy and reliable installation.
Cons:
Image is still quite large.
