Installing & running PandaRoot
==============================

raw.title: Installation process ¶
raw.text:
Installation process
¶
First you need to set the environment variables SIMPATH and FAIRROOTPATH, which are the folders where you have the installed the external packages and FairRoot. If the installation was done with Spack, both folders may be the same. On a cluster this may be already pre-installed for you, e.g. on a CVMFS.
export
SIMPATH
=
/home/pandauser/fairsoft_XXX/install
export
FAIRROOTPATH
=
/home/pandauser/FairRoot-vXX.X.X/install
Create a build directory and build PandaRoot:
mkdir build
cd
build
cmake ../PandaRoot
make -j4
You can change the
-j4
to the number of CPU cores you have available to speed up the process.
If your CMake installation on your system is too old, then the external packages installed a new one. You can use this line instead:
$SIMPATH
/bin/cmake ../PandaRoot

raw.title: Build PandaRoot ¶
raw.text:
Build PandaRoot
¶
Create a build directory and build the sources (here in ../source):
mkdir build
cd
build
cmake ../source
make -j4
You can change the
-j4
to the number of CPU cores you have available to speed up the process.
If your CMake installation on your system is too old, then the external packages installed a new one. You can use this line instead:
$SIMPATH
/bin/cmake ../PandaRoot
To setup PandaRoot in a new shell, just source the configuration script:
. build/config.sh -a
You can provide a flag -a to append or -p to prepend to the current PATH and LD_LIBRARY_PATH variables. Appending is the least invasive to your environment, prepend is to prefer installed executables & libraries form FairSoft, FairRoot and PandaRoot. Giving no option will overwrite the environment.

raw.title: Readme.md
raw.text:
# PandaRoot

This software is designed to the specific needs of the PANDA experiment. It is used to perform event generation, particle transport ("simulation"), detector digitisation and reconstruction, particle identification as well as event analysis.


### Installation
For **user installation** instructions please refer to [docs/Installation/Install_PandaRoot.md](docs/Installation/Install_PandaRoot.md)

If you do **development**, please follow the instructions in [docs/Installation/Install_Developers.md](docs/Installation/Install_Developers.md)

The installation at the **GSI cluster** Virgo is described in [docs/Installation/Install_GSI.md](docs/Installation/Install_GSI.md)

### Examples
To run a simulation chain with PandaRoot you can refer to `macro/master` which contains the most recent macros. More detailed examples and tutorials are found under `tutorials`. The most recent one is `tutorials/thailand2017`.

### Overview

There are many event generators, which can be found in `pgenerators`. The detector code is put at `detectors`. Under `geometry` the root geometries and related files are stored. 
The input and the parameters are located in `config`, `gconfig`, `input` and `macro/params`. Tracking and PID code is located in `tracking`, `genfit`, `genfit2` and `pid`. 
The analysis related classes are found in `analysis`. 
All data formats are separated from the actual algorithms and can be referenced in `pnddata`.

Under `macro/QA` you will find the quality assurance checks, which are performed each night. Their results can be found at [https://cdash.gsi.de/index.php?project=PandaRoot](https://cdash.gsi.de/index.php?project=PandaRoot).

CernVM-FS installation
¶
CernVM-FS was successfully installed on your Mac.cvmfs-config.cern.ch
There are only two steps necessary to access any repository:
Mount the CernVM-FS config repository:
• sudo mkdir -p /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
• sudo mount -t cvmfs /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
Mount a CernVM-FS repository using the following steps:
• sudo mkdir /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
• sudo mount -t cvmfs sft.cern.ch /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
Please note that from MacOS 10.15 Catalina is necessary to reboot your system after the installation in order to create the /cvmfs directory.
Enjoy!
Client configuration
¶
client
:
Install
cvmfs
using your distribution’s package manager.
Copy the
master public key
to
/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub
.
Place the repository-specific config file to
/etc/cvmfs/config.d/
. For GSI-internal repositories, use Stratum 0 (an HTTP proxy is usually used automatically on centrally managed GSI machines). For publicly reachable repositories, use Stratum 1.
Example for public repositories:
fairsoft.gsi.de.conf
:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
=
"http://cvmfs-s1.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY
=
"DIRECT"
CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY
=
"/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"
Example for GSI-internal repositories:
fairsoft.gsi.de.conf
:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
=
"http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY
=
"DIRECT"
CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY
=
"/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"
Instead of duplicating the repo name in the
CVMFS_SERVER_URL
, you can also use
@fqrn@
there like this:
CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/@fqrn@"
.
Mount the desired repository through any of the available mechanisms. Example for a systemd unit file
cvmfs-cvmfstest.gsi.de.mount
:
[
Unit
]
Description
=
Mount
/
cvmfs
/
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de
After
=
network
.
target
[
Mount
]
What
=
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de
Where
=/
cvmfs
/
fairsoft
.
gsi
.
de
Type
=
cvmfs
[
Install
]

multi

user
.

On OSX
¶
On Mac OS X, CernVM-FS is based on
macFUSE
. Note that as of macOS 11 Big Sur, kernel extensions need to be
enabled
to install macFUSE. Verify that fuse is available with
kextstat
|
grep -i fuse
Download the CernVM-FS client package
in
the terminal
in
order to avoid signature warnings

curl -o ~/Downloads/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg https://ecsft.cern.ch/dist/cvmfs/cvmfs-2.8.0/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg

sudo mount -t cvmfs fairsoft.gsi.de /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de/

raw.title: docs/Installation/CVMFS.rst
raw.text:
CernVM-FS installation
======================

CernVM-FS was successfully installed on your Mac.cvmfs-config.cern.ch
There are only two steps necessary to access any repository:

1.  Mount the CernVM-FS config repository:
    • sudo mkdir -p /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
    • sudo mount -t cvmfs /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
2.  Mount a CernVM-FS repository using the following steps:
    • sudo mkdir /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
    • sudo mount -t cvmfs sft.cern.ch /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
    Please note that from MacOS 10.15 Catalina is necessary to reboot your system after the installation in order to create the /cvmfs directory.
    Enjoy!

Client configuration
--------------------

**client**:

- Install ``cvmfs`` using your distribution's package manager.
- Copy the `master public key <https://git.gsi.de/dc/cvmfs-server/-/blob/16e98ee7bc5a7f70d395d8c8d4e3cdf1f83ef930/near-production/shared/masterkey.gsi.de.pub>`_ to ``/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub``.
- Place the repository-specific config file to ``/etc/cvmfs/config.d/``. For GSI-internal repositories, use Stratum 0 (an HTTP proxy is usually used automatically on centrally managed GSI machines). For publicly reachable repositories, use Stratum 1.

Example for public repositories:
``fairsoft.gsi.de.conf``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s1.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
  CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY="DIRECT"
  CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY="/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"

Example for GSI-internal repositories:
``fairsoft.gsi.de.conf``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
  CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY="DIRECT"
  CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY="/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"

Instead of duplicating the repo name in the ``CVMFS_SERVER_URL``, you can also use ``@fqrn@`` there like this: ``CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/@fqrn@"``.

- Mount the desired repository through any of the available mechanisms. Example for a systemd unit file ``cvmfs-cvmfstest.gsi.de.mount``:

.. code-block::
  
  [Unit]
  Description=Mount /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
  After=network.target
  
  [Mount]
  What=fairsoft.gsi.de
  Where=/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
  Type=cvmfs
  
  [Install]
  WantedBy=multi-user.target

On OSX
------

On Mac OS X, CernVM-FS is based on `macFUSE <http://osxfuse.github.io/>`_. Note that as of macOS 11 Big Sur, kernel extensions need to be `enabled <https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/change-startup-disk-security-settings-a-mac-mchl768f7291/mac>`_ to install macFUSE. Verify that fuse is available with

.. code-block:: bash
  
  kextstat | grep -i fuse
  Download the CernVM-FS client package in the terminal in order to avoid signature warnings
  
  curl -o ~/Downloads/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg https://ecsft.cern.ch/dist/cvmfs/cvmfs-2.8.0/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg
  Install the CernVM-FS package by opening the .pkg file and reboot. Future releases will provide a signed and notarized package.

Mount each time with

.. code-block:: bash
  
  sudo mount -t cvmfs fairsoft.gsi.de /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de/

Mount via Docker Container
--------------------------

The steps explained in the [previous section](#client-configuration) have been packaged into a docker image ``rklasen/cvmfs``. Running a container from this image provides FairSoft/FairRoot via CVMFS on the host at ``/cvmfs``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  docker run -d --name cvmfs --privileged --cap-add SYS_ADMIN --device /dev/fuse --volume /cvmfs:/cvmfs:shared rklasen/cvmfs

The container continues to run in background. Check after about a minute whether it works

.. code-block:: bash
  
  ls /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
  centos7  centos8  debian10  debian8  macos-10.15  ubuntu1804

raw.text:
If your CMake installation on your system is too old, then the external packages installed a new one. You can use this line instead:
$SIMPATH
/bin/cmake ../PandaRoot
Quick Running PandaRoot
¶
Each new shell needs to receive the proper environment variables, that PandaRoot can run. Simply load the
config.sh
which was created during the build process.
. Build/config.sh -p
Mind the space between the dot and the file name. You can provide a flag
-a
to append or
-p
to prepend to the current
PATH
and
LD_LIBRARY_PATH
variables. Appending is the least invasive to your environment, prepend is to prefer installed executables & libraries form FairSoft, FairRoot and PandaRoot. Giving no option will overwrite the environment.
Now you can call
root
, which has the appropriate version and the connection to PandaRoot. Execute any root macro, e.g:
cp -r PandaRoot/macro/master MyMacros
cd
MyMacros
root -l -b -q sim_complete
'(100, "TGeant3", 6.231552, "mytestsim")'
root -l -b -q full_complete
'(100, "mytestsim")'
In your
Build/bin
you will find a few executables, mainly some bare event generators for the use in the terminal, if necessary.

evidence.text:
CernVM-FS installation
======================

CernVM-FS was successfully installed on your Mac.cvmfs-config.cern.ch
There are only two steps necessary to access any repository:

1.  Mount the CernVM-FS config repository:
    • sudo mkdir -p /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
    • sudo mount -t cvmfs /cvmfs/cvmfs-config.cern.ch
2.  Mount a CernVM-FS repository using the following steps:
    • sudo mkdir /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
    • sudo mount -t cvmfs sft.cern.ch /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch
    Please note that from MacOS 10.15 Catalina is necessary to reboot your system after the installation in order to create the /cvmfs directory.
    Enjoy!

Client configuration
--------------------

**client**:

- Install ``cvmfs`` using your distribution's package manager.
- Copy the `master public key <https://git.gsi.de/dc/cvmfs-server/-/blob/16e98ee7bc5a7f70d395d8c8d4e3cdf1f83ef930/near-production/shared/masterkey.gsi.de.pub>`_ to ``/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub``.
- Place the repository-specific config file to ``/etc/cvmfs/config.d/``. For GSI-internal repositories, use Stratum 0 (an HTTP proxy is usually used automatically on centrally managed GSI machines). For publicly reachable repositories, use Stratum 1.

Example for public repositories:
``fairsoft.gsi.de.conf``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s1.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
  CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY="DIRECT"
  CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY="/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"

Example for GSI-internal repositories:
``fairsoft.gsi.de.conf``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de"
  CVMFS_HTTP_PROXY="DIRECT"
  CVMFS_PUBLIC_KEY="/etc/cvmfs/keys/masterkey.gsi.de.pub"

Instead of duplicating the repo name in the ``CVMFS_SERVER_URL``, you can also use ``@fqrn@`` there like this: ``CVMFS_SERVER_URL="http://cvmfs-s0.gsi.de/cvmfs/@fqrn@"``.

- Mount the desired repository through any of the available mechanisms. Example for a systemd unit file ``cvmfs-cvmfstest.gsi.de.mount``:

.. code-block::
  
  [Unit]
  Description=Mount /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
  After=network.target
  
  [Mount]
  What=fairsoft.gsi.de
  Where=/cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de
  Type=cvmfs
  
  [Install]
  WantedBy=multi-user.target

On OSX
------

On Mac OS X, CernVM-FS is based on `macFUSE <http://osxfuse.github.io/>`_. Note that as of macOS 11 Big Sur, kernel extensions need to be `enabled <https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/change-startup-disk-security-settings-a-mac-mchl768f7291/mac>`_ to install macFUSE. Verify that fuse is available with

.. code-block:: bash
  
  kextstat | grep -i fuse
  Download the CernVM-FS client package in the terminal in order to avoid signature warnings
  
  curl -o ~/Downloads/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg https://ecsft.cern.ch/dist/cvmfs/cvmfs-2.8.0/cvmfs-2.8.0.pkg
  Install the CernVM-FS package by opening the .pkg file and reboot. Future releases will provide a signed and notarized package.

Mount each time with

.. code-block:: bash
  
  sudo mount -t cvmfs fairsoft.gsi.de /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de/

Mount via Docker Container
--------------------------

The steps explained in the [previous section](#client-configuration) have been packaged into a docker image ``rklasen/cvmfs``. Running a container from this image provides FairSoft/FairRoot via CVMFS on the host at ``/cvmfs``:

.. code-block:: bash
  
  docker run -d --name cvmfs --privileged --cap-add SYS_ADMIN --device /dev/fuse --volume /cvmfs:/cvmfs:shared rklasen/cvmfs

The container continues to run in background. Check after about a minute whether it works

.. code-block:: bash
  
  ls /cvmfs/fairsoft.gsi.de

###############################################################################
## script for creating LMD data used for the fitting procedure etc.

batchjob=0

# directory of the data generated with dpm

  filelist_url=${filelist_path}/filelist_${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.txt

echo "data path: ${input_path}!"

if [ ! $numEv ]; then
  numEv=0

# if {filelist_url} is empty, the createLmdFitData binary must be run

  echo ${LMDFIT_BUILD_PATH}/bin/createLmdFitData -m $pbeam -t $type -c ${config_path} -d ${input_path} -n ${numEv} -e ${elastic_cross_section}

  fi
else
  echo $/build/bin/createLmdFitData -m $pbeam -t $type -c ${config_path} -d ${input_path} -f ${filelist_url} -o ${output_path} -n ${numEv} -e ${elastic_cross_section}
  if [ $batchjob -eq "0" ]; then
    ${LMDFIT_BUILD_PATH}/bin/createLmdFitData -m $pbeam -t $type -c ${config_path} -d ${input_path} -f ${filelist_url} -o ${output_path} -n ${numEv} -e ${elastic_cross_section} 2>&1 >> ${data_path}/createLumiFitData.log
  else

exit 0;

Impact of Target Profile Uncertainty
93
Figure 5.6: Modified Restgas profiles with ±10% density variations (orange and
green curves) compared to the nominal profile (blue curve).
The contrast between the consistent and mismatched scenarios leads to a critical
conclusion: The LuminosityFit framework is capable of high precision, but its ac-
curacy is strictly limited by the knowledge of the underlying longitudinal target
density profile 𝜌(𝑧).
A 3% systematic uncertainty induced by unnoticed Restgas variation is unaccept-
able. To mitigate this, one cannot rely on the LMD alone, as it cannot provide
the target profile including the Restgas background during data taking. Therefore,
an independent and precise measurement of the target and Restgas distribution is
required. This necessitates the use of the tracking systems in PANDA, particularly a
detector with high vertex resolution close to the interaction point.
This motivation leads directly to the next part of this thesis: the feasibility study
of using the tracking system of the PANDA Target Spectrometer in order to pre-
cisely measure the target density profile along the beam axis, including the Restgas
distribution.

def createLumiFitJob(experiment: ExperimentParameters) -> Job:
    # allocate two times this many cores on a compute node, or we'll get a segfault.
    # 16 seems to work when we allocate 32 cores, so just leave it like that. the fit
    # only takes like five minutes anyway
    number_of_threads: int = 16

    LMDscriptpath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitScripts
    LMDbinPath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitBuildDir
    elasticMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.dataPackage)
    resAccMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.resAccPackage)
    config_url = experiment.fitConfigPath
    lumiFileName = experiment.lumiFileName

    resource_request = JobResourceRequest(walltime_in_minutes=12 * 60)
    resource_request.number_of_nodes = 1
    resource_request.processors_per_node = number_of_threads
    resource_request.memory_in_mb = 2000

    # use either the reconstructed IP or the IP from the experiment config
    # (data package reco settings)
    # this is slightly hacky, but the runLmdFit binary can't read the experiment config.
    # so we're reading the experiment config ourselves and write a second recoIP.json file
    # that we're passing

    if experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.use_ip_determination:
        recoIPfile = experiment.recoIPpath
    else:
        recoIPfile = experiment.experimentDir / "recoIP-fromConfig.json"
        with open(recoIPfile, "w") as f:
            externalIPjson = {
                "ip_x": experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.recoIPX,
                "ip_y": experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.recoIPY,
            }
            json.dump(externalIPjson, f)

    job = Job(
        resource_request,
        application_url=f"{LMDscriptpath}/singularityJob.sh '{LMDbinPath}/bin/runLmdFit -c {config_url} -d {elasticMergeDataPath} -a {resAccMergeDataPath} -m {number_of_threads} -o {lumiFileName} -i {recoIPfile}'",
        name="runLmdFit",
        logfile_url=str(elasticMergeDataPath / "runLmdFit.log"),
        array_indices=[1],
    )
    return job

#!/usr/bin/env python3

"""
! DEPRECATION WARNING! This script is now superseded by the wrappers.lumifit module!
"""

"""
This script is a wrapper for runLmdFit and submits it to SLURM.

Two parameters are strictly required:
- fit config path
- data path

Is is however advised to also provide:
- resAcc path
- number of threads, ideally 16
- output file name INCLUDING path

TODO make this a module, have it return a job object! Then the dermineLuminosity function is the only one that actually submits jobs!
"""


import argparse
from pathlib import Path

from lumifit.cluster import ClusterJobManager, Job, JobResourceRequest
from lumifit.config import load_params_from_file
from lumifit.gsi_virgo import create_virgo_job_handler
from lumifit.himster import create_himster_job_handler
from lumifit.paths import generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath
from lumifit.types import ClusterEnvironment, ExperimentParameters

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
    description="Script for going through whole directory trees and looking for bunches directories with filelists in them creating lmd data objects.",
    formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter,
)

parser.add_argument(
    "-e",
    "--experiment_config",
    dest="ExperimentConfigFile",
    type=Path,
    help="The Experiment.config file that holds all info.",
    required=True,
)

args = parser.parse_args()

# load experiment config
experiment: ExperimentParameters = load_params_from_file(args.ExperimentConfigFile, ExperimentParameters)


# allocate two times this many cores on a compute node, or we'll get a segfault.
# 16 seems to work when we allocate 32 cores, so just leave it like that. the fit
# only takes like five minutes anyway
number_of_threads: int = 16

LMDscriptpath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitScripts
LmdBuildPath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitBuildDir
elasticMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.dataPackage)
resAccMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.resAccPackage)
config_url = experiment.fitConfigPath
lumiFileName = experiment.lumiFileName

resource_request = JobResourceRequest(walltime_in_minutes=12 * 60)
resource_request.number_of_nodes = 1
resource_request.processors_per_node = number_of_threads
resource_request.memory_in_mb = 2000

job = Job(
    resource_request,
    application_url=f"{LMDscriptpath}/singularityJob.sh '{LmdBuildPath}/bin/runLmdFit -c {config_url} -d {elasticMergeDataPath} -a {resAccMergeDataPath} -m {number_of_threads} -o {lumiFileName}'",
    name="runLmdFit",
    logfile_url=str(elasticMergeDataPath / "runLmdFit.log"),
    array_indices=[1],
)

# nay, return job!

if experiment.cluster == ClusterEnvironment.VIRGO:
    job_handler = create_virgo_job_handler("long")
elif experiment.cluster == ClusterEnvironment.HIMSTER:
    job_handler = create_himster_job_handler("himster2_exp")
else:
    raise NotImplementedError(f"Cluster type {experiment.cluster} is not implemented!")

# job threshold of this type (too many jobs could generate to much io load
# as quite a lot of data is read in from the storage...)
job_manager = ClusterJobManager(job_handler, total_job_threshold=2500)

# for job in joblist:
job_manager.enqueue(job)

raw.text:
Track Reconstruction and Event Preparation
63
Momentum Assumption The LMD, being a forward spectrometer without magnetic field in the tracking volume, cannot measure the momentum of the particles. However, for elastic scattering, the momentum loss of the forward scattered antiproton is negligible (Δ 𝑝 ≈ 100 keV /𝑐 at 1 . 5 GeV /𝑐 beam momentum and Δ 𝑝 ≈ 10 MeV /𝑐 at 15 GeV /𝑐 ). Therefore, the track momentum for the back-propagation is fixed to the nominal beam momentum 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 .
Track Transport GEANE numerically integrates the equation of motion through the detailed magnetic field map ⃗ 𝐵 ( ⃗ 𝑟 ), as illustrated in Figure 3.6. This transforms the track state ⃗ 𝑞 𝐿𝑀𝐷 to the vertex state ⃗ 𝑞 𝐼𝑃 .
The reconstructed scattering angle 𝜃 𝑟𝑒𝑐 is then defined as the angle between the backpropagated momentum vector 𝑝 ⃗ 𝐼𝑃 and the incoming beam axis (typically the 𝑧 -axis, or the tilted beam axis as discussed in Section 3.6).
Figure 3.6: Back-propagation of tracks from the LMD to the Interaction Point through the dipole, transition and solenoid fields using the GEANE track propagator. Figure adapted from [92].
Track Filtering and Selection
During the whole reconstruction process, several additional filtering stages are applied to ensure data quality:
Cleaning: 'Split Tracks' (a single particle reconstructed as two tracks) and 'Ghost Tracks' are removed based on shared hit criteria and 𝜒 2 quality cuts at the track finding stage.
Box Cut: Secondary particles produced in the beam pipe material or vacuum box frames typically originate from vertices far from the IP. By applying cuts on the reconstructed azimuthal ( 𝜑 ) and polar ( 𝜃 ) angles, a significant portion of this background is suppressed while maintaining high efficiency for the elastically scattered antiprotons. This filter is optimized before back-propagation and labeled as 'XY-Cut Filter' in Figure 3.5.

Simulations Macro
¶
Here is the simulation macro fromm
macro/master
:
macro/master/sim_complete.C
¶
PndMasterRunSim
*
fRun
=
new
PndMasterRunSim
();
fRun
->
SetInput
(
inputGenerator
);
fRun
->
SetName
(
SimEngine
);
fRun
->
SetParamAsciiFile
(
parAsciiFile
);
fRun
->
SetNumberOfEvents
(
nEvents
);
fRun
->
SetBeamMom
(
BeamMomentum
);
fRun
->
SetStoreTraj
(
kTRUE
);
fRun
->
SetOptions
(
options
);
// -----  Initialization   ------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
Setup
(
prefix
);
// -----   Geometry   -----------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
CreateGeometry
();
// -----   Event generator   ----------------------------------------------
fRun
->
SetGenerator
();
// -----   Event filter setup   -------------------------------------------
FairFilteredPrimaryGenerator
*
primGen
=
fRun
->
GetFilteredPrimaryGenerator
();
primGen
->
SetVerbose
(
0
);
// ---- Example configuration for the event filter ------------------------
// FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts* chrgFilter = new FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts("chrgFilter");
// chrgFilter->AndMinCharge(4, FairEvtFilter::kCharged);
// primGen->AndFilter(chrgFilter);
// -----   Add tasks   ----------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
AddSimTasks
();
// -----   Intialise and run   --------------------------------------------
fRun
->
Init
();
fRun
->
Run
(
nEvents
);
fRun
->
Finish
();
Quick Event Generator Setup
¶
There is an easy way to set the event generator by just a string. For detailed information on the event generators please refer to
Event Generators
EvtGen
Let the string end on
.dec
, which should point to a valid decay file. One may append a resonance name in the form of
:myResonance
to specify where EvtGen should start off. By default the top resonance is searched for in the decay file.
Background
The standard generic background is provided by the FTF model, which is enabled by starting the string with
ftf
. Similarly one can use DPM with
dpm
.
Particle Gun
Starting the string with
box
enables a particle gun, which can be configured right within the string.
Adding
type(pdgcode,mult)
specifies the particle type and number per event. Also the ranges for momentum (
p(min,max)
), theta (
tht(min,max)
), phi (
phi(min,max)
) and the starting point (
xyz(x,y,z)
) can be set.
As an example this is a single pion with 1 GeV/c that covers the barrel of the detector:
"box:type(211,1):p(1,1):tht(10,120):phi(0,360)"
Pythia8
Starting the string with
pythia8
will allow to use Pythia8 as a generator. A list of parameters may be attached to this string, separated by
;
which will be passed to Pythia8. Without providing any option, by default
SoftQCD:inelastic
=
on
is set.
ASCII file
If an external generator produced an ASCII file in the EvtGen format, one can include that by a string like
myFile.asc
PIPI Generator
The form of
pipi:cosTheta(min,max)
will enable this generator with some settings.
Lepton Pair Generator
Choosing a string in this form
leplep:pid(value):gegm(value):cosTheta(min,max)
enables the two lepton generator with its settings.
If one needs a custom generator or setting, there is always the option to skip the
fRun->SetGenerator();
statement and attach the custom generator by
fRun->AddGenerator(myGen)
.
Event Filter
¶
There is the possibility to filter out events before even attempting the simulation. This may save a lot of computing time as well as storage, if one for example ignores background events which could never pass the analysis selection of the signal.
Here is an example to have at least four charged particles in the event.
TString
generatorOptions
=
""
;
fRun
->
SetGenerator
();
// -----   Event filter setup   -------------------------------------------
FairFilteredPrimaryGenerator
*
primGen
=
fRun
->
GetFilteredPrimaryGenerator
();
primGen
->
SetVerbose
(
0
);
// ---- Example configuration for the event filter ------------------------
FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts
*

MasterTasks
¶
These classes serve as default settings for PandaRoot runs. They are steered by a prefix and option strings to keep the actual macros small and user-friendly. In the following part the available options are being described.
In general the prefix manages the file name splitting between the stages. A prefix called
"data/signal"
will set up the chain to produce files in the folder
data/
, relative to the current directory. These files will be called
signal_sim.root
,
signal_digi.root
,
signal_rec.root
&
signal_pid.root
, depending on which stages are being written to separate files. Also all parameters for this run will be stored in
signal_par.root
in the same directory.
Simulations Macro
¶
Here is the simulation macro fromm
macro/master
:
macro/master/sim_complete.C
¶
PndMasterRunSim
*
fRun
=
new
PndMasterRunSim
();
fRun
->
SetInput
(
inputGenerator
);
fRun
->
SetName
(
SimEngine
);
fRun
->
SetParamAsciiFile
(
parAsciiFile
);
fRun
->
SetNumberOfEvents
(
nEvents
);
fRun
->
SetBeamMom
(
BeamMomentum
);
fRun
->
SetStoreTraj
(
kTRUE
);
fRun
->
SetOptions
(
options
);
// -----  Initialization   ------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
Setup
(
prefix
);
// -----   Geometry   -----------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
CreateGeometry
();
// -----   Event generator   ----------------------------------------------
fRun
->
SetGenerator
();
// -----   Event filter setup   -------------------------------------------
FairFilteredPrimaryGenerator
*
primGen
=
fRun
->
GetFilteredPrimaryGenerator
();
primGen
->
SetVerbose
(
0
);
// ---- Example configuration for the event filter ------------------------
// FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts* chrgFilter = new FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts("chrgFilter");
// chrgFilter->AndMinCharge(4, FairEvtFilter::kCharged);
// primGen->AndFilter(chrgFilter);
// -----   Add tasks   ----------------------------------------------------
fRun
->
AddSimTasks
();
// -----   Intialise and run   --------------------------------------------
fRun
->
Init
();
fRun
->
Run
(
nEvents
);
fRun
->
Finish
();
Quick Event Generator Setup
¶
There is an easy way to set the event generator by just a string. For detailed information on the event generators please refer to
Event Generators
EvtGen
Let the string end on
.dec
, which should point to a valid decay file. One may append a resonance name in the form of
:myResonance
to specify where EvtGen should start off. By default the top resonance is searched for in the decay file.
Background
The standard generic background is provided by the FTF model, which is enabled by starting the string with
ftf
. Similarly one can use DPM with
dpm
.
Particle Gun
Starting the string with
box
enables a particle gun, which can be configured right within the string.
Adding
type(pdgcode,mult)
specifies the particle type and number per event. Also the ranges for momentum (
p(min,max)
), theta (
tht(min,max)
), phi (
phi(min,max)
) and the starting point (
xyz(x,y,z)
) can be set.
As an example this is a single pion with 1 GeV/c that covers the barrel of the detector:
"box:type(211,1):p(1,1):tht(10,120):phi(0,360)"
Pythia8
Starting the string with
pythia8
will allow to use Pythia8 as a generator. A list of parameters may be attached to this string, separated by
;
which will be passed to Pythia8. Without providing any option, by default
SoftQCD:inelastic
=
on
is set.
ASCII file
If an external generator produced an ASCII file in the EvtGen format, one can include that by a string like
myFile.asc
PIPI Generator
The form of
pipi:cosTheta(min,max)
will enable this generator with some settings.
Lepton Pair Generator
Choosing a string in this form
leplep:pid(value):gegm(value):cosTheta(min,max)
enables the two lepton generator with its settings.
If one needs a custom generator or setting, there is always the option to skip the
fRun->SetGenerator();

Event Filter
¶
There is the possibility to filter out events before even attempting the simulation. This may save a lot of computing time as well as storage, if one for example ignores background events which could never pass the analysis selection of the signal.
Here is an example to have at least four charged particles in the event.

generatorOptions
=
""
;
fRun
->
SetGenerator
();
// -----   Event filter setup   -------------------------------------------

*

=

->
GetFilteredPrimaryGenerator
();

->

(
0
);

=
new
FairEvtFilterOnSingleParticleCounts
(
"chrgFilter"
);

->

(
4
,

::
kCharged
);

->
AndFilter
(
chrgFilter
);
Beam & Target settings
¶
In the experiment the interaction region will be no ideal point at (0,0,0), but rather a distribution with a beam width and beam opening angle folded with the target material and residual gas along the beam line.
Event generators are able to handle those and the MasterTasks feature a few preset settings, which are accessed by an integer setting. For analysis which look for a realistic setting please choose
TargetMode 4
.
fRun
->
SetTargetMode
(
imode
);
TargetMode 0
(default):
All events originate from (0,0,0)
TargetMode 1
a cluster-jet sized beam-target region at the interaction zone
horizontal gaussian width of dx = 1 mm
FWHM length in beam direction of dz = 10 mm.
Target TDR, page 44
TargetMode 2
Pellet target sized beam-target at the interaction zone
horizontal gaussian width of dx = 3 mm
gaussian length in beam direction of dz = 3 mm.
At PANDA a beam diameter around 3mm is needed and one may want even smaller size when PTR is not possible.
Target TDR, page 61
TargetMode 3
Pellet beam-target at the interaction zone
horizontal gaussian width of dx = 0.2 mm
FWHM length in beam direction of dz = 0.2 mm.
A position resolution sigma(x, y, z) < 0.2 mm in the interaction position is desirable for event reconstruction.
Target TDR, page 61
TargetMode 4
Gaussian beam size of 2 mm
An opening of dr/dz=0.1 which matches the specifications of the “Fair Operation Modes” document v.6 (2020). The opening starts at the “edges” of the solenoid field, defined by the points of half field strength.
Realistic Target & rest gas density along the beam pipe (Apr. 2021)
input/restgasthickness_210421_Normal_IP_with_Cryopump.txt
TargetMode 5
Gaussian beam size of 2 mm
An opening of dr/dz=0.1 which matches the specifications of the “Fair Operation Modes” document v.6 (2020)
A flat profile along the beam (
input/H_flatprofile.txt
) for development purposes
TargetMode 6
No beam size distribution
A realistic profile along the beam (
input/restgasthickness_210421_Normal_IP_with_Cryopump.txt
) for development purposes
TargetMode 7
No beam size distribution
A flat profile along the beam (
input/H_flatprofile.txt
) for development purposes
Transport Model Options
¶
The transport model does calculation and simulation of the passage of particles through matter.
GEANT4 should be the default and can be activated through setting a string:
fRun
->
SetName
(
"TGeant4"
);
In order to use GEANT3 as transport model, choose
fRun
->
SetName
(
"TGeant3"
);
Mind, that GEANT3 has a code base where the algorithms are not being actively developed since a ling time. For most applications this should suffice.
Option String
¶
These options may be put in the option string.
"phase1"
Reduced setup for the whole Phase 1 of Panda, leaving out the RICH, the DISC
"day1"
Reduced detector setup for the first beam time, leaving out the RICH & the DISC, using only 2 GEM stations and a reduced FTS with stations 1-4.
With further parts to the string one can change the Day1 setup.
"strip"
or
"nopixels
Removes the Pixel part of the MVD in the Day1 setup
"gem0"
or
"nogem
Removes the GEM detectors
"gem3"
Will extend the Day1 setup to feature the full 3 GEM stations
"fts1256"
Here the FTS stations 4-5 are missing, and stations 5-6 are added

Digitization can be activated by
fRun->AddDigiTasks(kFALSE);
, which digitizes the simulated data. The flag switches the persistency of the digitized data. For analysis runs this can be switched off, if the reconstruction will be performed within the same run. This saves some disk space.
Local reconstruction, clustering and tracking is enabled by
fRun->AddRecoTasks(kFALSE)
. Also here a persistency flag decides wether the intermediate data is written to the files.
In the end the analysis object data is produced by
fRunt->AddPidTasks()
. This should be stored to disk in most cases.
In order to see which parts are being used in the digitization one may refer to the
PndMasterDigiTask
,
PndMasterRecoTask
and
PndMasterMultiPidTask
classes.
Option String for Digitization & Reconstruction
¶
These options may be put in an option string. For readability one should separate them, e.g. by semicolons.
"day1"
Reduced detector setup for the first beam time, leaving out the RICH digitization as well as the DISC PID
"phase1"
Reduced setup for the whole Phase 1 of Panda, leaving out the RICH digitization as well as the DISC PID
"fakeonline"
Emulating a worse tracking resolution by simple smearing of reconstructed tracks.
"nogem"
or
"gem0"
Deactivating the GEM processing as well as falling back to an older tracking code.
"nomc"
This option disables the ideal PID as well as the cloning of the MC truth tracks.
"multikalman"
This creates five times the tracking & PID chain for the hypotheses of the charged final state particle types
"electron"
,
"muon"
,
"pion"
,
"kaon"
&
"proton"
. Adding any combination of these particle type strings will restrict the reconstruction to those only, effectively speeding up the whole process.
"genfit2"
Using GenFit2 instead of the older version GenFit1
"newGF2"`
Using the new interface for GenFit2 with the faster Kalman algorithm instead of the older one. This feature will become the default in the next release.
"stttracking"
Fall back to an old track finding algorithm
"ftsca"
Use the CA tracking in the forward straws instead of ideal tracking. This feature will be discontinued with updated tracking code.
"ftstrack"`
Use PndFtsTracking for the forward straws instead of ideal tracking. This feature will become the default in the next release.
"goodtracks"
Add some track preselection before the PID.
For example a Lambda-Lambdabar channel analysis in Phase 1 of Panda could use this option string:
"phase1;multikalman;pion;proton;genfit2"

#!/bin/bash

NoOfEvents=200000
NoOfJobs=2
EventsPerJob=$(($NoOfEvents/$NoOfJobs))
while read line; do

	fNameChopped=${line%.root}
	echo $fNameChopped
    #echo $line
    
  subdir=COSY/Ana/ToCombine/${fNameChopped}
  path=${SIMDATADIR}/${subdir}
	if [ ! -d $path ]; then 
		mkdir -p $path
	fi
	
	JobLogPath=${SIMDATADIR}/${subdir}/joblogs
	if [ ! -d $JobLogPath ]; then 
		mkdir -p $JobLogPath
	fi

	AnaLogpath=${SIMDATADIR}/${subdir}/analogs
	if [ ! -d $AnaLogpath ]; then 
		mkdir -p $AnaLogpath
	fi

	jobpath=${SIMDATADIR}/${subdir}/jobs
	if [ ! -d $jobpath ]; then 
		mkdir -p $jobpath
	fi

	JobNo=0
	if [ line ]
	then
		for ((StartEvent=0; StartEvent<$NoOfEvents; StartEvent=$(($StartEvent+$EventsPerJob))))
		do
			JobNo=$((JobNo+1))
			fileAddition=${line}_StartEvent_${StartEvent}_NoOfEvents_${EventsPerJob}
			echo "StartEvent $StartEvent"
			cat >$jobpath/job_$fileAddition.sh <<EOF
			#!/bin/bash
			#
			#PBS -N ana_${JobNo}_$line
			#PBS -j oe
			#PBS -o ${JobLogPath}/0-job_$fileAddition.log
			#PBS -V
      #PBS -l nodes=1:ppn=1,walltime=24:00:00

			export PATH=\$PBS_O_PATH
			cd \$PBS_O_WORKDIR

			echo "Start Analysis of $line."
			root -l -q -b ../COSYBackgroundAnalysis.C\(\"$line\"\,$StartEvent\,$EventsPerJob\) &> $AnaLogpath/ana_$fileAddition.log


EOF
			echo "Analysis of $line"
### submit job to batch system
			qsub $jobpath/job_$fileAddition.sh
			echo "root -l -q -b ../COSYBackgroundAnalysis.C\(\"$line\"\,$StartEvent\,$EventsPerJob\) &> $AnaLogpath/ana_$fileAddition.log"
		done
	fi

done < ../../Lists/COSYSimulationsToAnaList.txt

raw.text:
Luminosity Determination with Restgas Distribution
77
Figure 4.4: Differential acceptance maps showing the subtraction of two adjacent acceptance maps of Figure 4.3.
Generation of the Effective Acceptance including Restgas
Instead of performing a complex numerical integration of the acceptance 𝜖 ( 𝜃, 𝑧 ) over the gas profile during the fit, a Monte Carlo Template approach is employed. That means, the acceptance, which is recalculated afterwards to get the effective acceptance in dependence on 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 , is directly derived from simulations incorporating the Restgas distribution. The step to get it calculated correctly is as follows:
Gas Profile Configuration: The event generator is configured to sample interaction vertices according to the extended target density profile as shown in Figure 4.2.
Full Simulation: These events undergo the complete detector simulation and reconstruction chain. This process naturally accounts for all geometric cuts, sensor edges, and efficiency variations experienced by particles originating from displaced vertices.
Effective Map Extraction: The effective acceptance 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) is then calculated as the ratio of reconstructed to generated events:
Crucially, this map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 is distinct from the standard point-source acceptance 𝜖 𝑝𝑜𝑖𝑛𝑡 used for the point-like interaction region. It contains the convolution of the extended target density distributions with the 𝑧 -dependent detector response.
Figure 4.5 shows the effective acceptance map derived from this procedure together with the acceptance map for the point-like interaction region. Compared to the point-source acceptance, the effective acceptance exhibits significant deviations. The point-source acceptance exhibits sharp boundaries and distinct efficiency drops corresponding to the gaps between sensor modules. This reflects the precise geometric projection of the detector as seen from the fixed center (0 , 0 , 0). In contrast, the effective acceptance necessary for the Restgas distribution displays significantly softer gradients. As the Restgas events originate from a range of 𝑧 positions, the projection of the sensor edges onto the angular plane ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) shifts continuously. The superposition of these shifted projections results in a blurring effect, effectively smoothing out the dead zones and module gaps. This visual comparison underscores the necessity of the usage of the Restgas background. If the sharp point-source acceptance map were used to model the background component, the fit would attempt to impose non-existent sharp structures onto the smooth background data. This mismatch would manifest as artificial residuals around the sensor edges, leading to a poor likelihood and, critically, a systematic bias in the extracted total luminosity. By employing the effective acceptance, the fit model correctly matches the smeared geometry of the experimental data, ensuring a robust and unbiased determination of ℒ 𝑖𝑛𝑡 . Therefore, the final fit model 𝜈 ( 𝜃 ) is constructed using this effective acceptance. In Equation 3.15, the geometrical acceptance map 𝜖 𝑖 is replaced by 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 ( 𝜃 𝑥 , 𝜃 𝑦 ) to generate the new fit model that accurately accounts for the extended target effects:

raw.title: li_2026 PDF page 82
raw.text:
Consequently, the antiproton beam interacts not only with the dense target but also with this low-density Restgas. Crucially, these Beam-Restgas interactions (¯ 𝑝𝑝 → ¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) are kinematically indistinguishable from the desired signal Beam-Target interactions, as they share the exact same final state particles and kinematics. The only spatial distinction between the two is the longitudinal position of the reconstructed interaction vertex, 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 . While the signal events are highly localized at the nominal interaction point ( 𝑧 ≈ 0), the Restgas background events are continuously distributed along the entire 𝑧 -axis of the beam pipe.
74
Luminosity Determination with Restgas Background
Figure 4.1: Schematic of the vacuum pump locations at PANDA close to the interaction point. Figure adapted from [137].
Spatial Density Distribution
The following study is based on the Cluster Jet Target developed by Münster Group, which is currently the default target option for PANDA. The PANDA Cluster Jet Target generates a directed stream of hydrogen clusters by expanding pre-cooled hydrogen gas through a fine Laval nozzle into the vacuum. The expansion creates a core jet of solidified hydrogen clusters. A system of skimmers and collimators is employed to geometrically define this beam, removing the majority of the uncondensed gas. Ideally, this results in a well-defined target density profile 𝜌 𝑗𝑒𝑡 with a transverse diameter of few millimeters to centimeters at the interaction point ( 𝑧 = 0). Due to the constant flow of the jet, the time-averaged density 𝜌 𝑗𝑒𝑡 ( 𝑧 ) is modeled as a flat distribution in the longitudinal direction, with a width 𝜎 𝑗𝑒𝑡 determined by the jet's geometrical intersection with the beam ( 𝜎 𝑗𝑒𝑡 = 2cm) [138].
However, despite the skimmers, a fraction of the hydrogen gas inevitably enters the scattering chamber. This arises from two mechanisms:
Gas Halo: Imperfect separation of the clusters from the carrier gas leads to a diffuse 'curtain' of hydrogen molecules accompanying the main jet.
Evaporation and Scattering: Clusters interacting with the beam pipe edges or evaporating during flight contribute to a continuous gas load.
The shape of the residual gas distribution 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) is governed by the dynamic equilibrium between the gas load from the target and the effective pumping speed at the interaction region. Due to the limited conductance of the narrow beam pipe and the placement of the vacuum pumps the gas density is not uniform.

Chapter8
Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

Luminosity Determination with Restgas Background
4.1 Realistic Target Distribution
While the beam properties discussed in the previous chapter primarily affect the angular resolution, the properties of the target introduce a spatial complexity that fundamentally challenges the point-like interaction assumption. In the PANDA fixedtarget setup, the interaction region is not confined to a dimensionless point but follows the density distribution of the gas molecules along the beam axis.
Origin of the Restgas
The primary interaction region in PANDA is a stream of frozen hydrogen pellets or a cluster jet, intersecting the antiproton beam at the nominal interaction point (IP, 𝑧 = 0). Ideally, the scattering process occurs exclusively within the geometric overlap of the beam and this target stream.
However, the injection of target material into the beam pipe inherently degrades the local vacuum quality. Despite the high-capacity pumping system, a fraction of the hydrogen target evaporates or scatters out of the main stream, creating a cloud of so-called Restgas. This gas accumulates within the scattering chamber and diffuses along the beam pipe until it is removed by the nearest vacuum pumps. Figure 4.1 shows the vacuum pump locations at PANDA close to the interaction point.
Consequently, the antiproton beam interacts not only with the dense target but also with this low-density Restgas. Crucially, these Beam-Restgas interactions (¯ 𝑝𝑝 → ¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) are kinematically indistinguishable from the desired signal Beam-Target interactions, as they share the exact same final state particles and kinematics. The only spatial distinction between the two is the longitudinal position of the reconstructed interaction vertex, 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 . While the signal events are highly localized at the nominal interaction point ( 𝑧 ≈ 0), the Restgas background events are continuously distributed along the entire 𝑧 -axis of the beam pipe.

For the PANDA experiment, luminosity is determined by measuring the rate of antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering, a reference process with a well-understood physical cross section [4]. While the theoretical framework for this reference channel is firmly established, its experimental realization faces severe challenges. Unlike standard collider experiments with highly focused interaction points (IP), PANDA operates with a fixed-target setup using a Cluster-Jet target. The intense hydrogen jet causes the evaporation of hydrogen into the surrounding beam pipe which is called the residual gas or Restgas distribution. Interactions between the antiproton beam and the Restgas create continuously distributed interaction vertices along the beam axis [5]. This phenomenon results in a complex, extended target profile that deviates significantly from an ideal point-like target. Previous reconstruction algorithms, which naively approximate the IP as an extended point at the coordinate origin [6, 7], are fundamentally insufficient for this complex geometric situation. Neglecting the extensive spread of the target profiles leads to severe systematic biases in the luminosity determination, ultimately limiting the achievable precision of cross section measurements and resonance scans.
2
Motivation
This thesis addresses these critical challenges by developing a comprehensive, datadriven methodology that transforms the Restgas distribution from an unknown, limiting background contribution into a precisely monitored and continuously measurable observable. Central to this approach is the refinement of the software framework to explicitly account for the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap through the introduction of an 'Effective Acceptance Map'. To constrain the dominant systematic uncertainties associated with the Restgas density profile, this work evaluates a hardware-driven solution: upgrading the PANDA Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with state-of-the-art High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS). Leveraging the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS alongside a specialized off-IP reconstruction chain, this thesis establishes the feasibility of extracting the longitudinal Restgas distribution directly from tracking data. By integrating this measured profile back into the luminosity determination, the systematic uncertainty is successfully suppressed to better than 0 . 5%. Ultimately, this research provides the robust luminosity determination essential for fulfilling the high-precision physics goals of the PANDA experiment, ensuring that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum and explore the fundamental nature of the strong interaction.

Limitations of the Standard Approach: In the standard PandaRoot workflow, a strong geometric constraint is imposed by assuming that particle trajectories originate from the beam axis near the nominal interaction point. As a result, tracks identified by the finder are processed by a Kalman Filter and typically propagated forward by ≈ 2 cm, then Kalman-fitted tracks are propagated to the point of closest approach to the 𝑧 -axis (POCA-to-line), which is then used to define the reference momentum vector and path length for the PID step.
124
Precise Measurement of the Restgas Distribution
While this approximation is well justified for interactions localized within the target region, it leads to significant systematic biases when applied to interactions with Restgas particles. Owing to the beam complication and the extended longitudinal density profile of the Restgas background, such interactions are distributed stochastically along the vacuum pipe and may exhibit substantial displacements in both transverse ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) and longitudinal ( 𝑧 ) directions. Forcing a helical trajectory to reference the beam axis when its true origin is displaced by several centimeters can result in severe reconstruction distortions. In particular, transverse offsets may cause the geometric solver to fail or produce ambiguous solutions, while longitudinal displacements lead to an incorrect estimation of the particle's flight path through the detector material. This path-length miscalculation directly affects the energyloss ( 𝑑𝐸/𝑑𝑥 ) correction and introduces a systematic bias in the reconstructed polar angle 𝜃 , as the momentum vector is effectively evaluated at an unphysical reference plane.
Modified POCA-First Approach: To address these topological limitations, a modified reconstruction scheme, referred to as the POCA-First Approach , was developed. Starting from the global track candidates seeded by the Apollonius finder and produced by the Kalman filter, the algorithm analytically computes the threedimensional point of closest approach (POCA) of all the tracks of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events. The resulting coordinate, ⃗ 𝑣 POCA , provides an estimator of the true interaction vertex and serves as the physical anchor point for subsequent kinematic reconstruction.
Once the geometric vertex ⃗ 𝑣 POCA is established, the Kalman-fitted tracks perform a targeted back-propagation. The track parameters are propagated from the outer detectors back specifically to the point of closest approach, to the 3D coordinate ⃗ 𝑣 POCA (POCA-to-point), rather than to the 𝑧 -axis. This POCA-to-point back-propagation effectively reconstructs the IP for displaced vertices, ensuring that the track parameters are evaluated at the actual interaction location. It is at this location that the momentum vector is evaluated, and the path length is determined for the energy loss calculation. This ensures that the PID algorithms receive kinematic inputs that correctly reflect the particle's history through the detector material and magnetic field up to the actual point of interaction.
By anchoring the track parameters to the reconstructed interaction vertex rather than an arbitrary axis, this approach effectively eliminates the systematic biases introduced by displaced vertices, thereby enabling accurate IP and momentum reconstruction and particle identification for events from beam-Restgas interactions. The validity of using this calculated geometric estimator was rigorously verified through simulation studies.

The studies in Section 5.4 have clearly demonstrated the necessity of a precise measurement of the target distribution along the beam axis. Furthermore, the simulation studies in Section 6.3 have established that the upgraded MVD with HV-MAPS technology provides the necessary hardware performance, specifically the excellent spatial resolution and low material budget, to resolve the longitudinal distribution of Restgas background. However, the hardware upgrade alone is insufficient to extract the Restgas profile with the precision required for luminosity determination. To achieve this, the precise measurement of the longitudinal target profile will be performed specifically utilizing antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering events, which serve as a high-statistics and kinematically well-understood reference channel.
A fundamental challenge lies in the event reconstruction algorithms. The standard reconstruction chain in the PandaRoot framework is primarily optimized for physics channels originating from the nominal IP at (0 , 0 , 0). Beam-Restgas interactions, however, are distributed along the entire beam axis, often extending centimeters or decimeters away from the IP. Applying standard tracking and particle identification (PID) routines to these displaced vertices introduces systematic biases, as track parameters and error matrices are typically propagated to the origin rather than the true interaction vertex. To overcome this limitation, a dedicated reconstruction algorithm tailored for shifted IP scenarios is essential. This algorithm must accurately account for the spatial distribution of the beam-Restgas interactions, ensuring that track fitting and vertex reconstruction are performed with respect to the actual interaction points rather than the nominal IP.

The accurate reconstruction of the interaction vertex distribution of the elastically scattered ¯ 𝑝𝑝 events which also originate by interactions of beam particles with Restgas profiles necessitates specialized algorithms capable of handling displaced vertices.

8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

7.3 Efficiency Analysis and Correction
The strategy described in the previous sections successfully reconstructed the IP of the single event, but the measured spectrum does not tell about the true physical density of the Restgas background. Due to the limited geometrical acceptance of the tracking system and the kinematic cuts applied during event selection, the detection probability varies significantly depending on the IP where the event originates. To extract the intrinsic Restgas profile 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ) from the raw reconstructed data, an efficiency correction must be applied.
Before establishing the correction function, it is essential to determine the necessary dimensionality of the efficiency map. Specifically, we must ascertain whether the detection efficiency 𝜀 exhibits a significant dependence on the transverse and longitudinal coordinates ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), which would necessitate a complex 3D correction map 𝜀 ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 ), or if a simplified 1D curve 𝜀 ( 𝑧 ) or even a constant 𝜀 0 suffices for the required precision.
To answer this question, a systematic simulation study was performed using the DPM generator to scan the interaction volume. Chapter5 Performance Studies for Luminosity
Determination with Restgas Background
Following the methodology established in Chapter 4, this chapter presents the comprehensive validation of the LuminosityFit software framework with Restgas background. The primary objective is to demonstrate that the extended target model allows for a precision luminosity determination (Δ ℒ / ℒ < 1%) even in the presence of significant Restgas background and realistic beam distortions.
The validation strategy follows a bottom-up approach:
Single Parameter Validation: Isolating individual beam effects (IP offset, Tilt, Divergence) to verify the robustness of the reconstruction against the extended background.
Fit Strategy Optimization: Establishing a stable iterative procedure to handle parameter correlations.
System Validation: Evaluating the final performance in realistic scenarios where all effects are superimposed, comparing the performance with and without the Restgas component.
To benchmark the algorithms, a series of Monte Carlo simulations were performed using the DPM Generator (to simulate realistic antiproton-proton elastic scattering events) and the Box Generator (to generate acceptance maps and resolution functions) in PandaRoot with the Cluster Jet target profile and the extended target model described in Section 4.1.

Determination of the Restgas Profile
Building upon the reconstruction algorithms established in Chapter 7, specifically the Apollonius tracking and the POCA-based vertexing, this chapter evaluates the final performance of the Restgas profile measurement. The primary objective is to extract the longitudinal density distribution, 𝜌 𝑔𝑎𝑠 ( 𝑧 ), from the reconstructed event rate. This process requires a rigorous handling of detector acceptance limits and, crucially, the correction of resolution effects arising from the extreme density gradients between the target and the Restgas background.
8.1 Definition of the Measurement Range
Unlike conventional analyses that focus solely on the immediate vicinity of the Interaction Point (IP), the Restgas determination requires a global perspective along the entire beam axis. The measurement range is explicitly defined as 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, a decision driven by the physical constraints of the PANDA vacuum system and the tracking detector layout. The upstream limit at 𝑧 = -3 . 0 m is determined by the location of the powerful cryogenic pump system in the beam line. As illustrated in the vacuum profile simulation (Figure 3.14), the Restgas density drops by several orders of magnitude beyond this point due to the effective pumping, rendering the gas contribution physically negligible. Similarly, the downstream boundary at 𝑧 = +6 . 0 m is constrained by the geometrical acceptance of the Forward Tracker (FT), which features its last two layers at 𝑧 = 6075mm and 𝑧 = 6545mm. Tracks originating significantly beyond this point cannot produce sufficient hits to form reconstructible candidates. Crucially, the vacuum distribution studies indicate that this defined region contains more than 99% of the total integrated Restgas density. Consequently, the distribution measured within this global range effectively represents the complete Restgas profile required for the luminosity determination, thereby eliminating the need for model-dependent extrapolations outside the detector acceptance.

8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

For the PANDA experiment, luminosity is determined by measuring the rate of antiproton-proton (¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) elastic scattering, a reference process with a well-understood physical cross section [4]. While the theoretical framework for this reference channel is firmly established, its experimental realization faces severe challenges. Unlike standard collider experiments with highly focused interaction points (IP), PANDA operates with a fixed-target setup using a Cluster-Jet target. The intense hydrogen jet causes the evaporation of hydrogen into the surrounding beam pipe which is called the residual gas or Restgas distribution. Interactions between the antiproton beam and the Restgas create continuously distributed interaction vertices along the beam axis [5]. This phenomenon results in a complex, extended target profile that deviates significantly from an ideal point-like target. Previous reconstruction algorithms, which naively approximate the IP as an extended point at the coordinate origin [6, 7], are fundamentally insufficient for this complex geometric situation. Neglecting the extensive spread of the target profiles leads to severe systematic biases in the luminosity determination, ultimately limiting the achievable precision of cross section measurements and resonance scans.
2
Motivation
This thesis addresses these critical challenges by developing a comprehensive, datadriven methodology that transforms the Restgas distribution from an unknown, limiting background contribution into a precisely monitored and continuously measurable observable. Central to this approach is the refinement of the software framework to explicitly account for the complex, smeared geometry of the beam-Restgas overlap through the introduction of an 'Effective Acceptance Map'. To constrain the dominant systematic uncertainties associated with the Restgas density profile, this work evaluates a hardware-driven solution: upgrading the PANDA Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) with state-of-the-art High-Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS). Leveraging the significantly reduced material budget of HV-MAPS alongside a specialized off-IP reconstruction chain, this thesis establishes the feasibility of extracting the longitudinal Restgas distribution directly from tracking data. By integrating this measured profile back into the luminosity determination, the systematic uncertainty is successfully suppressed to better than 0 . 5%. Ultimately, this research provides the robust luminosity determination essential for fulfilling the high-precision physics goals of the PANDA experiment, ensuring that the deviation in the luminosity determination will not limit the experiment's ability to map the exotic hadron spectrum and explore the fundamental nature of the strong interaction.

5.4 Impact of Target Profile Uncertainty
The results in the previous sections demonstrate the excellent performance of the luminosity determination, even if restgas background is present. Here, the assumption was made that the true Restgas distribution is perfectly known and correctly modeled in the Monte Carlo generation of the effective acceptance map. However, in the real experiment, Restgas may not be the same as the gas flow simulation of the target group predicts. Due to technical limitations or environmental changes, the vacuum conditions may fluctuate, leading to changes in the Restgas density or profile shape.
To quantify the systematic risk associated with these fluctuations, a sensitivity study was performed. Scenarios where the actual Restgas density deviates by ± 10% from the nominal expectation are considered, while the density in the target area ( -1 cm < 𝑧 < +1cm) remains constant, as shown in Figure 5.6.
Two distinct analysis approaches were applied to these modified datasets to evaluate the impact of model consistency:
Consistent Model: The modified profile of the Restgas is assumed to be known correctly and is incorporated into the analysis. The effective acceptance map 𝜖 𝑔𝑎𝑠 𝑒𝑓𝑓 used for the fit is updated to match the modified target density.
Mismatched Model: The more realistic case is chosen here where the change in the Restgas density is not noticed. The data contains the ± 10% variation, but it is fitted using the original effective acceptance map, simulating a model mismatch.
The results of both scenarios are summarized in Table 5.5. As expected, when the effective acceptance map matches the physical reality, the framework adapts perfectly. 3.6 Effects of Beam Properties
In the ideal mathematical description of elastic scattering, the interaction occurs at a singular point (0 , 0 , 0) and the antiproton beam vector is perfectly aligned with the 𝑧 -axis. However, the realistic PANDA beam conditions at the HESR introduce geometric and kinematic deviations. To achieve the target precision for the luminosity determination, these effects must be rigorously modeled to avoid systematic biases. They can be categorized into deterministic mean shifts, shift and tilt as illustrated in Figure 3.10, and stochastic broadening (Divergence). The IP Offset , shown in green, shifts the primary vertex position away from the nominal detector center, thereby breaking the azimuthal symmetry of the tracks. Furthermore, the Beam Tilt , shown in blue, causes a systematic angular deviation that strongly depends on the azimuthal angle 𝜑 .
IP Offset and Distribution
The interaction zone is defined by the spatial overlap of the antiproton beam and the target stream. This creates a distributed source rather than a point source. The framework treats the mean position (Offset) and the profile width of this distribution differently based on the detector's sensitivity. A transverse displacement ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 ) of the beam breaks the azimuthal symmetry of the detector acceptance. To determine this offset precisely, the Back-Propagation procedure is exploited as described in Section 3.4. After extrapolating the reconstructed tracks through the magnetic field back to the target region, the geometrical origin of each track is determined by calculating its Point of Closest Approach (POCA) to the nominal coordinate origin (0 , 0 , 0). The spatial distribution of these POCA points reflects the beam spot profile smeared by the resolution from reconstruction precision. Nevertheless, the Mean of this distribution provides the mean interaction vertex ( 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 0) with high precision ( 𝒪 (10 𝜇 m)). This measured position is then used to define the 'Beam Reference Frame'. All reconstructed quantities are calculated relative to this physically determined center, effectively removing the systematic bias induced by the beam offset.

Chapter4
Luminosity Determination with Restgas Background
4.1 Realistic Target Distribution
While the beam properties discussed in the previous chapter primarily affect the angular resolution, the properties of the target introduce a spatial complexity that fundamentally challenges the point-like interaction assumption. In the PANDA fixedtarget setup, the interaction region is not confined to a dimensionless point but follows the density distribution of the gas molecules along the beam axis.
Origin of the Restgas
The primary interaction region in PANDA is a stream of frozen hydrogen pellets or a cluster jet, intersecting the antiproton beam at the nominal interaction point (IP, 𝑧 = 0). Ideally, the scattering process occurs exclusively within the geometric overlap of the beam and this target stream.
However, the injection of target material into the beam pipe inherently degrades the local vacuum quality. Despite the high-capacity pumping system, a fraction of the hydrogen target evaporates or scatters out of the main stream, creating a cloud of so-called Restgas. This gas accumulates within the scattering chamber and diffuses along the beam pipe until it is removed by the nearest vacuum pumps. Figure 4.1 shows the vacuum pump locations at PANDA close to the interaction point.
Consequently, the antiproton beam interacts not only with the dense target but also with this low-density Restgas. Crucially, these Beam-Restgas interactions (¯ 𝑝𝑝 → ¯ 𝑝𝑝 ) are kinematically indistinguishable from the desired signal Beam-Target interactions, as they share the exact same final state particles and kinematics. The only spatial distinction between the two is the longitudinal position of the reconstructed interaction vertex, 𝑧 𝑣𝑡𝑥 . While the signal events are highly localized at the nominal interaction point ( 𝑧 ≈ 0), the Restgas background events are continuously distributed along the entire 𝑧 -axis of the beam pipe.

The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m.
